articles.title_orig: Stock market today: Dow, S&P 500, Nasdaq waver ahead of midterm election results, AMD earnings
articles.title_zh: Stock market today: Dow, S&P 500, Nasdaq waver ahead of midterm election results, AMD earnings
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
US stocks were mixed as Americans went to the polls for the midterm elections and braced for more AI industry earnings from Advanced Micro Devices ( AMD ).
The Dow Jones Industrial Average ( ^DJI ) fell 0.3%, while those on the S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) rose 0.5%. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite ( ^IXIC ) advanced by 0.8% following a turbulent day for chip stocks.
This evening, investors will watch the election results and ballot initiatives for insights into potential policy changes on key issues affecting markets, including pharmaceuticals, the housing market, and AI data centers.
But before then, AMD will report earnings after the closing bell, giving investors another glimpse of AI demand at a precarious time for the artificial intelligence trade. As Intel's ( INTC ) stock demonstrated last week , the market's reaction is likely to depend as much on Q4 guidance as on the company's top- and bottom-line results in the most recent quarter.
Apple ( AAPL ) stock fell in early trading following its own earnings report, which showed several bright spots (iPhone sales) but also some misses (Greater China revenue). Palantir ( PLTR ) stock also fell post-earnings despite results that beat expectations.
While earnings season continues apace, the Labor Department release its monthly Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey (JOLTS) report, showing openings and hiring changed little in September continuing the labor market's "low hire, low fire" trend.
Monday's close left chip stocks in a fresh bear market, below their summer lows and a key technical level. Tuesday, they're bouncing back like they want to make the bears regret it, Yahoo Finance Jared Blikre reports:
The PHLX Semiconductor Index ( ^SOX ) finished Nov. 2 about 22% below its Oct. 6 high, its second bear market since June. It was also the index's second straight close below its 200-day moving average , a line it hadn't closed under since June 2025, and its lowest close since April.
Nearly every chip and storage stock in the S&P 500 rose in early trading Tuesday, led by memory and chip-equipment names, and the index climbed back above its July 29 low. If chips can hold that ground, Monday's breakdown starts to look like a bear trap — a break below a key level that quickly reverses, catching traders who bet on more losses.
CrowdStrike ( CRWD ) said Tuesday that it has agreed to buy two AI security startups, Yahoo Finance's Ines Ferré reports:
CrowdStrike said it has signed an agreement to acquire Fiddler AI, a startup that develops tools that help companies track their AI systems.
The company also announced an agreement to acquire Dreadnode, a startup that develops tools to test AI systems for security vulnerabilities. CrowdStrike said the technology will allow its Falcon platform to continuously scan AI models, applications, and agents for potential security weaknesses before they are deployed.
The combined purchase price for both is $495 million , according to the Wall Street Journal. Shares of the cybersecurity company gained more than 2% in early trading.
Gas and diesel prices are the highest they have ever been on any Election Day in US history, according to Patrick De Haan, GasBuddy head of petroleum analysis.
The national average price for a gallon of gasoline is now $4.14, while a gallon of diesel is $6.29, according to AAA .
Higher prices, especially for fuel, are a key source of voter frustration heading into the polls on Tuesday.
Futures on Brent crude ( BZ=F ), the international benchmark, fell roughly 1% to trade around $104 per barrel Tuesday morning, whereas US WTI crude ( CL=F ) broke the $100 mark on Monday and is now trading around $96, down 6% from five days ago.
Brent crude ended October at a six-month high amid concerns that the conflict will reescalate following the midterm elections. The pullback from that peak comes as hopes return to the market over talks of a potential ceasefire between the US and Iran.
US stocks opened mixed Tuesday as investors awaited midterm election results and more AI-related earnings to come.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average ( ^DJI ) fell 0.4%, while the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite ( ^IXIC ) advanced by 0.3% following a turbulent day for chip stocks. Meanwhile, the S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) was up slightly.
Investors will watch election results Tuesday evening for potential shifts in policy around areas including housing, pharmaceuticals, and AI infrastructure. Before then, Advanced Micro Devices ( AMD ) reports after the bell, offering another read on AI demand after a sharp sell-off in chip stocks.
Apple ( AAPL ) and Palantir ( PLTR ) also traded lower following their earnings reports, along with pharmaceutical maker Pfizer ( PFE ) and e-commerce platform Shopify ( SHOP ).
Shopify ( SHOP ) stock plunged 15% in premarket trading on Tuesday after reporting third quarter results that missed the mark on several key metrics.
The cloud-based e-commerce platform's Q3 revenue of $3.74 billion came in just shy of consensus estimates of $3.75 billion for the first time since 2022, according to Bloomberg data. Subscription revenue for the quarter of $836 million also missed Wall Street expectations of $850.2 million, raising concerns about growth in its main recurring-revenue business.
Gross merchandise volume, or the total dollar value of orders sold through Shopify's platform, was $119.15 billion, also falling short of estimates of $120.08 billion.
Shopify's adjusted earnings per share of $0.49 topped estimates of $0.48.
Yahoo Finance's Brian Sozzi sat down with Binance co-founder Changpeng Zhao, better known in crypto circles as CZ , after hackers took roughly $6.3 billion worth of digital assets from the world's largest cryptocurrency trading platform .
"It's been a pretty hectic process," Zhao said of the aftermath of the hack. "But the good thing is right now the withdrawals have been restored, the systems back to normal. People are free to use the platform without any issues now. And then all user funds are covered. The users did not suffer any loss."
Sozzi writes that Binance moved swiftly to stabilize the situation by guaranteeing full customer restitution, deploying corporate treasury reserves, Secure Asset Fund for Users (SAFU) capital, and insurance funds to replenish user balances.
"There's no 100% security," CZ added. "So when you run a platform, especially a crypto platform the possibility is always there. I did not think it was going to be this big of magnitude, probably not."
Yahoo Finance's Ben Werschkul reports:
Prediction markets and pollsters both say Democrats are favored to take both the US House and Senate on Tuesday. But prediction markets are a little less certain about it, especially on the Senate side.
That's setting up what could be another chapter in the burgeoning rivalry between prediction markets and polls following 2024's closely watched results. The upper chamber is where the differences are most evident.
A small but consistent gap has been evident for months in the odds of Democrats taking control of the Senate. The gap has averaged about 7.4 percentage points since Sept. 1, according to a Yahoo Finance analysis
It sat at 7.2 percentage points on Monday, with three prediction markets placing a 73.1% chance of Democrats taking control while two polling-based models suggested the chances are higher at 80.3%.
Yahoo Finance's Hamza Shaban writes for today's Morning Brief newsletter:
It's not easy forking over more than $1,000 for a new iPhone every couple of years. But Apple ( AAPL ) has proved yet again that complaining about prices isn't the same thing as being unwilling to make the purchase.
The company reported its quarter on Monday after the bell, posting revenue that grew 12% last quarter and beating Wall Street's expectations. The company also beat on earnings per share.

articles.title_orig: Beijing launches diplomatic flurry amid threat of renewed U.S. war with Iran
articles.title_zh: Beijing launches diplomatic flurry amid threat of renewed U.S. war with Iran
articles.content_orig:
Beijing launches diplomatic salvo to woo Gulf leaders and bolster its influence in the region
China has held a flurry of meetings with Gulf leaders in a sign that Beijing is stepping up its diplomatic efforts in the Middle East.
The diplomatic salvo comes before a highly anticipated meeting between Donald Trump and Xi Jinping when the US president is expected to attend the Apec conference in Shenzhen, China, on 18 and 19 November.
Xi held talks with Haitham bin Tariq , Oman’s sultan, in a historic state visit to Beijing on Monday.
President Xi’s foreign minister, Wang Yi, met Saudi Arabia’s national security adviser, Musaad bin Mohammed Al Aiban, and the deputy secretary of Iran’s national security council, Ali Bagheri Kani.
Haitham’s trip to Beijing is the first time that an Omani head of state has visited China since the two countries established diplomatic relations nearly 50 years ago. According to a Chinese readout of the meeting, Xi warned that the Middle East should not become an arena for “great power rivalry and geopolitical conflicts”.
He said: “China has always been actively committed to stopping conflict and promoting peace, and hopes to contribute wisdom and solutions to resolving the regional security dilemma.”
Wang said after his separate talks that China was willing to “play a constructive role in helping the region emerge from the shadow of the pandemic and achieve lasting peace and stability”. In his meeting with Bagheri Kani, Wang said China supported Iran “in safeguarding its sovereignty and security”. According to China, the Iranian official said his country looked forward to China “playing a more important role in international and regional peace”.
When the US and Israel launched joint strikes on Iran in February, China was credited with pushing Tehran toward ceasefire talks in Pakistan , bolstering its status as a regional mediator.
Beijing’s influence in the Middle East is “no longer what it used to be”, said Shen Dingli, a Shanghai-based scholar of international relations. But he added: “Given China’s increased investment and trade in the region … its influence cannot be ignored.”
As the war has dragged on, China’s diplomatic efforts have been muted. Its biggest economic leverage over Iran is the fact that it buys about 90% of the Middle Eastern country’s crude oil exports. Between April and June, it slashed its crude imports by 30%, with the total in June plunging to the lowest level in a decade. That saved the global economy from a major spike in inflation. According to some estimates, China’s cut in oil imports shaved $30 or more off barrel prices of Brent crude, a global benchmark.
Beijing has otherwise done little to broker peace in the Middle East. That is partly because it does not see the conflict as being its responsibility to resolve. In March, Wang said the war “should never have happened” and that the US and Israel would find “no popular support” for the strikes.
China is also a beneficiary from the damage that the fighting has done to the US’s global reputation.
According to findings published in July by the Pew Research Center, a Washington-based thinktank, China is now viewed more favourably than the US in a majority of 36 countries surveyed.
The pain caused by the long-term disruption to the strait of Hormuz, the waterway through which much of the world’s oil and gas flows, also poses a risk to China’s economy. Shortages of energy cause inflation, which risks reducing global demand for Chinese goods.
Tehran and Washington are locked in intensive talks to reach an agreement, which could include reopening the strait. Trump has repeatedly threatened to renew military action against Iran after Tuesday’s midterm elections in the US, a move which would cause alarm in Beijing.
Trump’s desperation to reach a deal in the Middle East may also provide an opportunity for China to present itself as a regional peacemaker, bolstering Xi’s status before their meeting. Beijing brokered a detente between Saudi Arabia and Iran in 2023 but since then its diplomatic impact in the region has been limited.
Shen said China’s desire to improve diplomatic relations with Middle Eastern countries as well as the US were “mutually reinforcing” trends.
China’s foreign ministry spokesperson, Mao Ning, said on Monday that China would send special envoy Zhai Jun to Iran, Oman and Saudi Arabia in early to mid-November.

articles.title_orig: MTA should eliminate some jobs to prepare for budget woes, watchdog writes
articles.title_zh: MTA should eliminate some jobs to prepare for budget woes, watchdog writes
articles.content_orig:
Make your contribution now and help Gothamist thrive in 2026. Donate today
Gothamist is funded by sponsors and member donations
In less than four years, the MTA could be looking at a nearly $900 million funding shortfall as spending outpaces fare revenue, according to a new analysis from the Citizens Budget Commission, which recommends cutting the workforce to close the gap.
The budget watchdog recommends sweeping job cuts to positions that it argues technology has made obsolete. The budget commission suggested the MTA allow its trains to run with just one worker, instead of two.
Train lines that have new computer-based signals, like the L and the 7, are already fully automated, as are the announcements on the trains. While the conductor opens and closes the train doors, the operator has few other duties, which include hitting a button every 20 seconds to signal they are alert. The budget commission cited the operator’s limited responsibilities as a sign the job could be cut with no impact to service.
Eliminating operator jobs on the L and 7 lines could save $36.5 million a year, according to the report . If the agency moved to phase out two people operating trains across the system, it could save $500 million a year.
The agency is in the process of installing new signals on other lines like the A, C, E, F, G, M and R lines. For now, those lines still require two people to run the trains.
The suggestion from the Citizens Budget Commission comes at a sensitive time as Transport Workers Union Local 100 negotiates a contract with the MTA for its 40,000 subway and bus workers. The MTA is expected to release its financial plan for next year in the coming weeks, which will include a 4% fare and toll increase. The board will vote on that plan in December.
“The same recommendations have been coming down for dozens of years, so there's nothing new about it,” said Transport Workers Union of America President John Samuelsen. “It's essentially a recommendation to balance alleged deficits that the MTA has off the backs of working people.”
Last year, the state legislature tried to enshrine a requirement of two MTA workers on each train into law, but Gov. Kathy Hochul vetoed the bill , leaving open the possibility that one-person train operations could happen in the future.
“Legislatively mandated staffing prevents the MTA from modernizing — as technology and best practices continue to improve — and realizing the efficiency and financial benefits,” the Citizens Budget Commission's report argues.
The Citizens Budget Commission acknowledges the MTA has become more efficient in recent years, saving a reported $576 million this year through what the agency calls “operating efficiencies.” But the report argues that without cutting labor and healthcare costs, the MTA faces a $300 million budget gap next year that will grow to $900 million by 2030. The budget commission estimates its recommended reforms could save $2.5 billion annually.
Other recommendations include streamlining fare collection on the commuter railroads by checking tickets prior to boarding, reducing the need for someone to walk through the train. The Citizens Budget Commission argues cutting more than 1,000 jobs on Metro-North and the Long Island Rail Road could save $380 million annually.
The report also recommended MTA retirees pay more in healthcare premiums, which could bring in an additional $315 million a year.
Samuelsen countered that many laborers, ironworkers, track workers, and crane operators in the MTA get paid less than their peers in the private sector, but accept that because of the generous retirement benefits.
"The CBC is right to note that we've made extraordinary progress in securing hundreds of millions of dollars in new recurring operational efficiencies," MTA spokesperson Mitch Schwartz wrote in a statement. He did not address the proposal to eliminate jobs.
Stephen Nessen covers transportation. Since 2008 he has reported on everything from Occupy Wall Street, the rebuilding of the World Trade Center site, Hurricane Sandy, to Trump’s campaign for president. His transportation reporting has taken him everywhere from the MTA’s secret Rail Control Center to the gleaming subways of Seoul. Got a tip? Email [email protected] .

articles.title_orig: Binance customers withdraw $7.4 billion after crypto heist
articles.title_zh: Binance customers withdraw $7.4 billion after crypto heist
articles.content_orig:
Binance customers withdrew $7.4 billion from the cryptocurrency exchange after it suffered what security experts said was the largest digital coin theft ever .
On Monday, a Binance spokesperson said customers also deposited $2.7 billion after the company allowed people to resume transactions on Sunday for Bitcoin, Ethereum and other cryptocurrencies, resulting in a net outflow of $4.7 billion in the company's holdings.
Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange with more than 300 million users, said the value of crypto holdings being withdrawn represents just 3% of its $157 billion in total assets.
"The net outflow is a relatively limited portion of Binance's overall asset base," the Binance spokesperson said in an email. "Withdrawal levels are stabilizing to what we would consider normal and expected on-chain activity."
The fund withdrawals came after cybercriminals, whom the FBI linked to North Korea, stole $6.3 billion in digital currency from Binance.
North Korea denies involvement in the attack. On Tuesday, Kim Yo Jong, the sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, called the FBI announcement "a trite provocation" and "an absurd rhetoric."
"This is not the first time that the U.S. has attempted to spread misunderstanding of the DPRK in the international community, blindly linking the DPRK with the 'cyber crime' incidents whenever they occur on an international scale," she said in a statement, using the abbreviation of North Korea's official name, the Democratic People's Republic of Korea.
Roughly $3 billion of the stolen assets were frozen, according to Binance. Freezing crypto funds allows certain issuers to block the transfer of their tokens anywhere in the world.
The hacker group believed to be responsible for the attack, known as "TraderTraitor," was converting most of the stolen assets into Ethereum in a move to hide their tracks, the FBI said Saturday. TraderTraitor was also responsible for a February 2025 attack on another crypto exchange, Bybit, that resulted in a $1.5 billion loss, according to the FBI.
Following the Binance attack, the FBI encouraged private-sector entities "to block transactions with or derived from addresses TraderTraitor actors are using to launder these stolen assets."
Binance has promised to cover the full losses using company funds. By early Sunday morning, it said it had covered around 95% of the impacted amount.
The Associated  Press contributed to this report.

"Our goal is simple: provide school leaders the control and confidence to use AI products in classrooms as they see fit," Google added.
Google also released a 29 page PDF on AI in Education .

articles.title_orig: Beyond screens: Mercedes-Benz’s new holographic heads-up display
articles.title_zh: Beyond screens: Mercedes-Benz’s new holographic heads-up display
articles.content_orig:
Do screens in cars represent luxury? Judging by the latest car interiors, the answer would seem to be an emphatic “yes.” Screens aren’t just getting larger; they are multiplying across the dashboard and morphing into different forms and concepts. Indeed, an interior’s screens are a pretty good indicator of what brand made the car—or at least how much the owner paid for it.
But is this actually what customers want ? Are more screens really better? And even if they are, luxury car features inevitably trickle down to cheaper, more mainstream offerings, and screens can only get so big. That leaves luxury automakers with another question to answer: “What’s next?”
Mercedes-Benz is working on a new display alternative that could provide an answer. For now, it’s known as the holographic display. Forget the images from Star Trek and Star Wars that just popped into your head, though. It’s effectively a more advanced form of heads-up display, or HUD.
Whereas a traditional HUD projects images onto the windshield glass, the holographic display has two main components. It still uses a projector, but its key element is a special transparent film laminated into the glass. The film uses holographic optical elements, or “super-small mirrors,” as Mercedes development engineer Lena Hees described them, that selectively reflect the light emitted by the projector, keeping the image visible even in direct sunlight while hiding it from the driver’s view.
Today, the passenger-side touchscreens in Mercedes and other luxury vehicles rely on driver-monitoring cameras or screen polarization to keep the driver from seeing what is playing on the passenger side.
Speaking of passenger screens, the holographic display is clearly being considered as a future alternative or replacement for this technology. Although screens in cars are increasingly ubiquitous, a recent JD Power study indicated that car owners classify passenger screens as “ not necessary ” and have generally negative opinions about them. Mercedes has clearly observed similar opinions but for slightly different reasons.
“We have customers who like the Hyperscreen,” said development engineer Maximilian Hilger of the pillar-to-pillar screen found in an increasing number of Mercedes models. “But there are others who want to maintain luxury materials.”
In other words, the massive screen design doesn’t seem as luxurious as the pillar-to-pillar bands of wood or other materials found in previous-generation models. And that’s not an opinion isolated to Mercedes’ customers.
New Mercedes chief design officer Bastian Baudy recently told German magazine Auto Motor Sport that “Materiality and haptics must remain tangible—with switches, buttons, and intuitive controls. Real materials are at the heart of Mercedes: metal, wood.”
Mercedes CEO Ola Källenius went further, grouping interior quality and materials among the brand’s “forever values,” along with safety and maintaining what a Mercedes is like to drive.
That presents conflicting priorities, however.
“Yes, you need to have all the [technology] that a customer could ever dream of and wants,” Källenius told Ars. “But you need to package it in an aesthetically pleasing way. That’s also part of it.”
That brings us back to the holographic display. Keep in mind that the photos in this article show early prototypes I saw at Mercedes’ research facilities in Sindelfingen, Germany. The prototype projector sits inside a rather crude, trapezoidal hole dug into the dash of a right-hand-drive, pre-2027 S-Class. It’s also loud, with a cooling fan whirring like a laptop visiting too many junk-filled websites.
The production version would have a much smaller projector opening than those of the prototype and existing heads-up displays. Manual Holstein, a manager working in Mercedes research for future displays, indicated that the projector could be small enough to be hidden behind wood or metal trim pieces. Holstein also said you won’t hear a fan in the production model and that the resolution would improve.
The resolution is certainly considerably better than any current head-up display, including Mercedes’ own, which features augmented reality elements . Full-color, commercial-like videos of the C-Class Electric played during the demonstration, and the display was sufficiently bright, even though Holstein said the prototype was operating at just 20 percent of its maximum brightness.
Issues remain, however. The resolution may be good compared to the arrows, script, and graphics of a current HUD, but it’s poor when compared to a passenger touchscreen. The video’s contrast was also too high, and as you can see in the photos, the picture was distorted into a narrow height due to the angle of the windshield. Frankly, no one would choose to watch anything on it over a phone, tablet, or conventional passenger screen. It needs to improve by orders of magnitude before becoming a viable alternative.
Again, though, this is just a prototype. Holstein said the holographic film size, or “eyebox,” can be made much bigger and be raised higher than the HUD-like height of the prototype. He also dismissed the distortion as a problem unique to the prototype.
Imagine nearly half the windshield transformed into a virtual screen that’s visible only to the passenger. Beyond videos or other entertainment, Mercedes envisions the holographic display highlighting points of interest in the view through the windshield. A similar display could be placed on the driver side, showing situational information, enabling video calls, or providing entertainment when parked. In the future, it could even let drivers watch things other than the road when Mercedes’ Level 3 autonomous driving system allows them to take their eyes off it. At the very least, the technology could replace today’s HUDs and their larger projector boxes.
Having experienced the prototype while the car was moving, I also think the holographic display could help prevent the motion sickness that can come from staring at a passenger screen while the car is moving. The higher screen angle and ability to see more of the outside world beyond created a notably different visual experience.
Of course, the question remains: “Is this what customers want?”
If the JD Power survey found that customers don’t care about passenger touchscreens, will they be any more enthusiastic about holographic video displays? That seems doubtful. But that’s just as much of an open question as whether the production version will actually live up to its promises.
There’s also another matter: What, exactly, defines luxury? Before Bastian Baudy took over as Mercedes’ chief design officer this year, his predecessor and former boss Gordon Wagener echoed Källenius’ thoughts about the direction of the brand’s interiors. He was considerably blunter, though.
“Screens are not luxury,” Wagener told ABC News . “You have a better—and bigger—TV at home, right? And every car has a big screen. So we have to create luxury beyond the screen. That’s why I talk about craftsmanship and sophistication.”
If the holographic display lets automakers emphasize traditional design and materials while still offering unique technology, it could be a promising way forward.

articles.title_orig: The 2026 iPad Mini is a terrific tiny tablet — for a big price
articles.title_zh: The 2026 iPad Mini is a terrific tiny tablet — for a big price
articles.content_orig:
With better performance and a better screen, this is a Mini to be reckoned with. But it’s not perfect, and it sure isn’t cheap.

With better performance and a better screen, this is a Mini to be reckoned with. But it’s not perfect, and it sure isn’t cheap.
If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.
The iPad Mini sometimes feels like a trap. It is, in some ways and for some people, the perfect iPad: meaningfully larger than my phone’s screen but still small and light enough to use for reading in bed or gaming on the subway. As most of the rest of the iPad line has tilted ever closer to laptop territory, the Mini might be the most iPad-y iPad left. I’ve taken a Mini everywhere with me since the very first one. But Apple only updates the Mini sporadically, and those updates sometimes feel like someone inside Apple Park picked its specs by closing their eyes and clicking randomly in an Excel sheet. The Mini is always a little underpowered, a little overpriced, and a little afield in Apple’s tablet lineup. We, the iPad Mini People, sometimes feel a little forgotten.
This year’s model , though, is an upgrade through and through. Apple made the screen larger and better, while making the iPad itself smaller and lighter. It upgraded the processor in a big way. It made the whole package more durable, so you can take it to more places and use it for more things. It actually feels like a tablet made for a reason, not just another occasional bone thrown to the small-tablet fans.
For the past week, I’ve been testing the midnight iPad Mini with cell service, 512GB of storage, and the nano-texture matte display coating. I really like it. It’s the best iPad Mini yet, and a huge leap over the previous model . The one in my hands also costs $1,249, and I cannot in good conscience tell you to buy it. Even the very cheapest version — Wi-Fi only, 128GB of storage, regular OLED display — starts at $699, by a wide margin the highest starting price ever for a Mini.
If you don’t already know the iPad Mini is your one true love, there’s probably a better iPad out there for you. But if you’re an iPad Mini Person and you can stomach the price? You’re getting the best Mini in years.
The Mini’s new display is its most important and most controversial upgrade. It now measures 8.5 inches instead of 8.3, and it’s now a 2316 x 1512 OLED panel instead of an LCD. The OLED gives the screen a little more dynamic range than the previous model, with brighter bright spots and darker dark spots. Its peak brightness is noticeably brighter than before, and its minimum brightness is low enough to be totally pleasant for reading in the dark (as long as you’re in dark mode). In general, it’s just a little more crisp and contrast-y, in a nice way; the old Mini’s display was the least of my worries, but the OLED is a solid improvement. The tablet I tested also has Apple’s nano-texture matte finish , which seems to dull and darken the screen slightly; on a particularly white background, the whole thing seems to shimmer. I suspect I’d like the OLED panel even more without it.
The nano-texture does, however, do an excellent job of reducing glare. The effect is actually really cool: The textured coating doesn’t extend to the bezels, so you can see a source of light or glare come in from the edge of the screen and then simply disappear as it hits the screen. So what you lose in pure screen fidelity, you gain in the ability to read on the iPad in a coffee shop without it reflecting the overhead lights like a mirror. The nano-texture option costs an extra $100, though, and requires you to upgrade to 256GB of storage, so you’re now looking at a $900 tablet. Spend the extra money on the cellular version or, better yet, don’t spend it at all.
For some reason, Apple has never deigned to put its ProMotion display tech on the iPad Mini, which has a refresh rate capped at 60Hz rather than the 120Hz you’ll get on most other recent Apple devices. This is such an odd spec choice that it has launched a bunch of conspiracy theories. Maybe it’s to make more people buy an iPhone Duo instead? Maybe it’s a 120Hz panel downgraded to 60Hz by software just to make people upgrade again next time? Apple’s answer, to Chris Lawley and others, has been something to the effect of “120Hz is irrelevant, OLED’s faster pixel response solves the problems.” I don’t agree. I don’t think the lack of ProMotion is an immediate and total dealbreaker, but refresh rates matter ! To games and high-touch creative apps, of course, but you notice the difference even with basic swiping and zooming. The Apple Pencil feels more juddery moving across my screen. On a 120Hz screen, I can scroll a browser page and still clearly read the text as it’s moving. With 60Hz, it gets blurry. In all these cases, even if you don’t explicitly see the difference, you really do feel it.
The most meaningful upgrade in the new Mini, at least for me and how I use my iPad, is that it is designed to be more or less waterproof and dustproof. Its IP67 rating means that the Mini got the highest possible score for protection from “solid foreign objects,” which for our purposes mostly just means dust won’t get inside, and is also “protected against the effects of temporary immersion in water.” It’s not quite as rugged as, say, the iPhone 18 Pro, and I don’t recommend using it as an underwater camera or anything, but your tablet should be fine as long as you don’t drop it in the tub and leave it for a while.
This increased ruggedness immediately changed my iPad usage in a couple of ways. I became less worried about handing the Mini to my toddler, whose general stickiness and penchant for spilling things no longer feel like threats. I also started using the Mini more in the kitchen — I love to cook with an iPad nearby for recipes and Community episodes, and it was nice not to be constantly guarding against flour explosions and water spills. At one point, the iPad Mini even came with me in the shower during a particularly close football game. It’s still kicking.
This is, for lack of a better word, the Field iPad.
The Mini’s IP rating is also the feature that finally made me see who Apple sees as the ideal iPad Mini user. This is, for lack of a better word, the Field iPad. We hear all the time about pilots who use Minis instead of sheaves of paperwork, but Apple also sees them in use on construction sites, oil rigs, doctor’s offices, and all kinds of other places. (It’s a fun rabbit hole, actually — can I interest you in an “explosion proof” last-gen Mini for $4,500 or so?) Apple’s goal with the Mini is not really to maximize performance, satisfy the pixel-peepers, or enhance creator workflows. It’s durability and usability. Body and screen.
Apple made a couple of changes to the Mini to receive its IP rating, like ditching the speaker holes and opting for what it calls an Acoustic Display. It means the sound fires out of the front panel rather than from speaker holes. (Some TVs currently work the same way.) It doesn’t sound any better than before, maybe a tiny bit bassier, but it also doesn’t sound worse, and if anything it’s slightly better to have the sound actually pointed at you instead of out the sides of the tablet. Mostly it’s a wash in service of the ruggedization, which is good enough for me.
The rest of the hardware is just wins all the way around. The A20 Pro chip, the chipset also on the iPhone 18 Pro (and the Duo ), benchmarks about 50 percent faster than the 2024 Mini for standard computing tasks, and about three times as fast for graphics-intensive ones. (The chip in my review unit has one more CPU core than the A20 Pro in the cheaper Minis; those will still be drastic improvements, but maybe a hair less so.) I notice the difference, even side by side with the old model, in how fast apps load and games play. Games like Assas

articles.title_orig: Detentions, resignations, probes shake Serbia after students toppled strongman Vucic in election
articles.title_zh: Detentions, resignations, probes shake Serbia after students toppled strongman Vucic in election
articles.content_orig:
I was wrong. Until October 25, when Serbia’s students won an extraordinary victory in an early general election, I thought they had little chance of bringing down Aleksandar Vučić, their country’s authoritarian leader. For the last two years I had followed as the students created a leaderless movement and selected candidates for an electoral list to run against Vučić and his party in a vote that he had called. All this was interesting, I thought. But Serbia was constantly witnessing bouts of protest, and it seemed hard to imagine that such a broad-church movement—one that sought to unite conservative and religious nationalists, left-wing liberals, and everyone in between—could unseat a party that had the power to give pensioners a bonus payment just before an election, compel public-sector workers to cast ballots for it at the risk of losing their jobs, or pay people for images of their ballot slip with the right name circled.
And yet the students won, not narrowly but by a crushing margin. After the Serbs toppled their wartime leader Slobodan Milošević, in October 2000, Georgians, Ukrainians, Egyptians, and others seeking to bring down their own dictators and autocrats studied the Serbian case or received training in how to do so from a Belgrade organization that claims to have worked in fifty-two countries since then. Now that young people are taking to the streets in France, India, and Albania, following a year of youth protests in countries as diverse as Nepal and Madagascar, I think we can bet that the demand for Serbs as consultants and trainers in unconventional methods of leader-toppling will boom again.
The current wave of student protest in Serbia began on November 1, 2024, when a recently renovated canopy at Novi Sad station collapsed and killed sixteen people. Corruption was alleged, along with official neglect. On November 22 students and professors who had gathered for a memorial to the victims at Belgrade University’s Faculty of Dramatic Arts were assaulted by thugs, probably paid for or linked to Vučić’s Serbian Progressive Party (SNS). The attack galvanized students across the country, who now took the lead in organizing protests and vigils and shutting down classes.
So far, so routine. Vučić, a minister under Milošević, and his party had been in power since 2012, and every year for the last decade there have been protests for one reason or another—against plans for lithium mining, plans to develop Belgrade’s waterfront, plans for Jared Kushner to develop the NATO-bombed former General Staff building in Belgrade into a luxury hotel, and so on. Over the years these had few if any results. But in the aftermath of the Novi Sad disaster the government appeared rattled and apprehensive.
Over the winter the protests grew smaller but did not fizzle out. Then, on March 15, 2025, some 300,000 people gathered to protest in Belgrade. Independent media called it the largest-ever protest in Serbian history. During the protest there was a sudden panic and many began to flee. Independent outlets quickly reported that the police had used a crowd-control “sound cannon” known as a Long Range Acoustic Device. According to the student movement’s manifesto, the sounds they heard and the “shockwave” caused the crowd to scatter: “civil society organizations collected over 3,000 testimonies from people describing the same moment and the physical distress that followed.” The authorities denied the use of the sound canon, which would have been illegal. This only enraged and energized the movement more. To publicize the cause, one group of students cycled to Strasbourg; another ran 1,200 miles to Brussels. Pro-Vučić thugs continued to attack protesters in bouts of violence, and the pro-government media more or less ignored what was happening. But the students kept going.
In November 2025 thousands of demonstrators turned out in Belgrade to protest a new law speeding along Kushner’s hotel development. The following month Kushner pulled out of the scheme after Serbia’s prosecutor for organized crime charged the minister of culture, among others, with falsifying documents in order to revoke the building’s status as a protected cultural monument. That such a thing could happen to a minister showed that things were already beginning to change, I was told by Slobodan Markovich, a historian at Belgrade University who is close to the student movement.
Much of middle-class, educated Serbia loathes Vučić and his party. In classic Balkan mode, the SNS is a vast patronage machine: until now many jobs in the public sector depended on membership. Much of the judiciary and media fell under party control, too. Ivan Vejvoda, a political scientist who began demonstrating as a student in 1968 and has witnessed or participated in many of the major events in Serbia’s history ever since, summed it up in a recent essay . Under Vučić, he wrote, “people lived for years in a captured state where they witnessed corruption, nepotism and clientelism every day.”
At the same time, he noted, organized crime has been “laundering enormous amounts of money” in the construction business, which offers easy opportunities to clean dirty funds. Much research has been done to reveal the link between Balkan drug trafficking groups and the construction boom of the last few years. In 2015 Darko Šarić, the head of a notorious international cocaine smuggling gang, was jailed. At a subsequent trial for money laundering the court heard how the group would, according to the judgement, invest their money in real estate, among other things. It was no surprise that the students’ main slogan this election was “Serbia or the Mafia.”
Vučić’s was not a dictatorship that murdered its opponents or threw them in jail for years. Its rule has been much more subtle. The journalist Jelena Petković told me how, in 2018, she was slowly but surely pushed out of her newspaper when it started falling in line with the regime, not least by simply ignoring stories that editors knew would annoy Vučić and the party. Zoran Kusovac, another journalist, told me a revealing anecdote. He asked an old friend of his why she had divorced her husband, who had a high-ranking job at a major government-supporting TV channel. “The main reason,” she said, was that every night, “as we were lying in bed, Vučić called to analyze the evening news bulletin and what was good and what was not good and what he wanted for tomorrow.”
February 15 is Serbian Statehood Day. It celebrates the moment in 1835 when Serbian leaders and several thousand prominent men and village heads from across the country adopted its first constitution in Kragujevac, seventy miles south of Belgrade. The death of Yugoslavia devastated that town, the home of a car and arms maker called Zastava. Things are much improved nowadays. Fiat builds cars in a modern plant there and Serbia exports arms around the world, including to Israel and Ukraine.
At a rally the students convened in Kragujevac to mark the day this year, I met a history student named Katarina Draganovic. I said that the energy seemed to be draining from the protests after fifteen months. “It is not about demonstrations anymore,” she replied. Students were fanning out across the country now, going to every town and village, and asking people “about their problems and what they want us to focus on when we win.”
In some ninety university and higher education departments, student “plenums” were debating ideas and selecting experts from among academics, medics, engineers, farmers, actors, and others. The movement had first called for an early general election in May 2025, and by December they had started collecting signatures on a petition for one. Eventually the students would select 250 of the experts to be on their list of candidates for parliament—what would be called the Student List. None of these experts had political backgrounds. Nor, however, were any of them students. The movement eschewed the idea of having any

articles.title_orig: Saudi Aramco Profit Jumps Despite Damaging Attacks on Pipelines and Refineries
articles.title_zh: Saudi Aramco Profit Jumps Despite Damaging Attacks on Pipelines and Refineries
articles.content_orig:
Aramco reported a 9% rise in third-quarter adjusted net income on Tuesday on stronger refining margins.
The Saudi oil giant posted adjusted net income of $31.2 billion for the quarter, up from $28.6 billion a year earlier. The figure exceeded the median analyst consensus estimate of $30.66 billion, according to the company.
Aramco's downstream business, which processes crude oil into fuels and other products, posted adjusted earnings before interest and taxes of $10.3 billion, up 234% from a year earlier, driven by stronger refining margins.
"Geopolitical uncertainty and attacks on key energy facilities continued to amplify the global energy supply crisis in the third quarter of 2026, with serious implications for global energy security," Aramco CEO Amin H. Nasser said in a statement.
Nasser said the company's operational flexibility and supply network enabled it to continue delivering energy to customers despite the disruptions. Aramco is also exploring additional overseas storage capacity and alternative export routes to strengthen its global supply network.
The company generated $28.2 billion in free cash flow during the quarter, up from $23.6 billion a year earlier.
Aramco said its board declared a third-quarter base dividend of $21.9 billion, up 3.5% year on year, to be paid in the fourth quarter.
The company also said its major upstream projects remained on track and highlighted its acquisition of a 49% stake in Saudi artificial intelligence company HUMAIN.
– CNBC's Emma Graham contributed to this story.

articles.title_orig: Russia confirms new Ukraine peace talks as Melania Trump prepares to host ceasefire meeting
articles.title_zh: Russia confirms new Ukraine peace talks as Melania Trump prepares to host ceasefire meeting
articles.content_orig:
Russia on Tuesday confirmed that peace talks with Ukraine and the U.S. will go ahead next week in Abu Dhabi, while also signaling that a meeting between Presidents Vladimir Putin , Donald Trump and Xi Jinping to end the conflict was on the table.
Putin aide Vladimir ​Medinsky will serve ⁠as Moscow's chief negotiator ​at the talks in Abu Dhabi on Nov. 10-11, Kremlin spokesman ​Dmitry Peskov told reporters on a conference call, according to Reuters.
Separately, First Lady Melania Trump will bring Russian and Ukrainian representatives to the White House to discuss the local ceasefire in Kherson, the White House said Tuesday.
Monday saw the end of a six-day ceasefire in the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky and surrounding areas in the Kherson region to allow for evacuation of residents, in a pause of hostilities that the White House said was brokered by the first lady.
Ukraine on Monday accused Russia of using the ceasefire to reinforce its military positions in the city.
The first lady's summit on Thursday will be "an extraordinary moment in American history," the White House said, but did not name the representatives who will attend. Melania Trump will deliver remarks on the Oleshky ceasefire at 11 a.m. ET Thursday, it added.
Peskov also said Tuesday the Kremlin hopes to finalize plans for a trilateral meeting between the leaders of Russia, the U.S., and China in the coming days. The comments follow earlier reports that these countries were planning to negotiate an end to the war in Ukraine, without Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy at the table.
Zelenskyy has said that any negotiations over Ukraine's future must include Kyiv.
"It can be acceptable only when we are at the table of negotiations," he said on Oct. 20, adding that he had discussed the proposal of a three-way meeting between the U.S., China, and Russia to negotiate an end to the nearly five-year full-scale war. "Nothing about Ukraine without Ukraine," he said.
Tensions between the U.S. and Ukraine have mounted over recent weeks amid continued strikes between Moscow and Kyiv, including on civilian and energy targets.
A series of moves by the Trump administration in October raised questions about Washington's reliability as Kyiv's most important military partner.
Tuesday's announcement follows U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff saying late Monday that Washington will mediate Ukraine-Russia peace talks in Abu Dhabi on Nov. 10-11, focusing on security arrangements, de-escalation and humanitarian issues.
Witkoff also said that U.S. negotiators will meet European and NATO officials in Brussels this week to discuss post-war security guarantees and Ukraine's reconstruction.

articles.title_orig: Europe on alert after supermarket freezers hit by cyber-attacks in nine countries
articles.title_zh: Europe on alert after supermarket freezers hit by cyber-attacks in nine countries
articles.content_orig:
A spate of cyber-attacks that hit supermarket chains across at least 10 European countries on Monday has prompted European Union officials to warn of a deliberate attempt to disrupt the food supply chain.
Supermarkets have reported problems in Belgium, Estonia, Finland, Ireland, Italy, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Portugal, Germany and Sweden, and the significant increase in freezer temperatures has forced retailers to discard food.
Temperatures in chains across Europe reportedly rose as high as 50C (122F).
No-one has yet admitted carrying out the cyber-attacks.
The European Union has raised concerns about the attacks, which come three weeks after a cyber-attack disrupted as many as 700 French grocery stores, causing food losses estimated at tens of millions of euros.
The security of refrigeration systems as well as other devices that can be monitored remotely has heightened concerns about government-backed hybrid attacks.
The EU's food and agriculture commissioner, Christophe Hansen, said the bloc was taking the incidents very seriously and warned of further disruption in the future.
Commission spokesman Thomas Regnier was careful not to attribute blame, but said: "These incidents of course show once again how cyber-attacks can disrupt essential services and affect citizens' daily lives."
"These are not isolated incidents and of course we have to be collectively resilient and prepared for such cyber incidents."
In Italy , Giorgia Meloni's government called a meeting with intelligence chiefs, but said the impact was "currently very limited" and most of the food distribution chain had up-to-date security systems able to fend off such attacks.
At least four Co-op supermarkets in Sicily and one business in Tuscany were affected, according to the national cybersecurity agency.
Meloni's office said those businesses affected were "mostly still equipped with obsolete security systems, with interfaces directly exposed to the internet and inadequate authentication mechanisms".
Belgian supermarkets were among those hardest-hit, with dozens of stores reporting refrigeration failures. Federal prosecutors have opened an investigation.
Mathieu Tilman, a manager at a Delhaize supermarket in Belgium, said he was shocked by this kind of attack: "I don't even understand how anyone could do this... How can we end up throwing away so much food? I find it truly distressing. In moments like these, you just feel like quitting your job."
In Ireland , 13 SuperValu stores were impacted by what the chain's owner, Musgrave Group, called a cyber-incident. "Replenishment of chilled and frozen ranges in the affected stores is well under way," a spokesman said on Monday.
A small number of corner shops in the Netherlands also suffered disruption. Last month, supermarket chain Albert Heijn had to take several services offline because of a separate cyber-attack.
There was disruption to refrigeration systems at the Rewe Büsken supermarket in western Germany after a cyber-attack on system provider Danfoss, the company told the BBC. Its systems have been back in operation since Monday afternoon.
In Portugal , the Mosqueteiros group said that incidents at seven Intermarché stores had been linked to a cyberattack, which "appears to have targeted an external service provider responsible for managing the refrigeration systems".
Swedish chain ICA also said "a limited number" of its stores had experienced refrigeration problems, without confirming a cyber-attack, and Sweden's national cyber-security agencies said they were monitoring the incident.
In Finland , irregular temperatures were detected in a few smaller grocery stores belonging to the Kesko group, which said it was investigating the issue.
In Estonia , at least one supermarket was attacked by hackers who raised the temperature in the refrigeration units to 50C, public broadcaster ERR reported.
In the UK , the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) has warned British retailers to update the software on fridge temperature controls.
The agency said the country was likely to suffer an AI-powered cyber-attack on critical national infrastructure within two years.
Richard Horne, the head of the National Cyber Security Centre, told BBC Radio 4's Today programme there were a couple of instances in the UK where "vulnerable technology has been exploited" after the cyber-attacks.
"We don't know the full impact, but we do know there are a couple of instances where vulnerable technology has been exploited and we're working with those organisations."
Asked if there was any evidence that supermarkets in Britain or freezers of the same make or model had been targeted, Horne said: "It's not just supermarkets, it's through the whole food supply chain, and we've been working through the night alerting organisations where we can see they've got exposed technology that's vulnerable in this way."

articles.title_orig: Santoli: AI bull market almost surely needs tech stocks to recover to keep advancing
articles.title_zh: Santoli: AI bull market almost surely needs tech stocks to recover to keep advancing
articles.content_orig:
Get Mike Santoli's Market Memo in your inbox first. SUBSCRIBE HERE
The road to bull-market glory does not run through Walmart and Berkshire Hathaway and Eli Lilly.
There's been a virtual buying panic in traditionally defensive, high-quality stocks over the past few weeks, a near-equal-and-opposite offset to the selling pressure in semiconductors and AI-build-out spenders. The three stocks above — the only members of the $1 trillion market-cap club not in Big Tech – have collectively added $550 billion in market value in the past month, almost making up for what Alphabet has lost.
The Nasdaq-100 and the S&P 500 Low Volatility ETF (SPLV) are rushing toward one another in a satisfying picture of symmetry that nonetheless reflects an almost comical level of tactical rotation executed by an investment community accustomed to playing one factor against another.
While this to-and-fro has so far protected the S&P 500 as a whole from an appreciable setback for months, it has left it stymied around levels that date back to May — before we got two earnings-reporting seasons showing 30% annual profit growth.
A week ago here , I suggested the AI theme was nearing a make-or-break moment to stage a recovery or risk surrendering its leadership status and destabilizing the broader market. Thus far, this trade has failed to respond to moderate oversold conditions or a run of cosmetically strong hyperscaler quarterly results, further loosening its grip on the benefit of the doubt.
In stressed markets undergoing soul-searching about the long-term bullish thesis, prices often need to travel further to find buyers with conviction while the market action must disappoint dip-buyers to extinguish complacency. Hard to know if we're there, but presumably we're now closer.
The Nasdaq-100 closed Monday right at its 200-day moving average, off almost 11% from its record high. After an enervating failed Monday-morning bounce attempt, the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index finished down another 3.8% and settled under the late-July low that was set as the Situational Awareness hedge fund was finished liquidating.
"Markets did not get the memo that bearish seasonal pressure typically subsides in mid-October and instead ended the month with some of the most acute selling pressure that has been realized during the late-summer/early-fall period," notes JPMorgan technical strategist Jason Hunter. He's advising clients to remain on the defensive "until we see clear evidence of a bottoming process on the charts or until there are clear signs of capitulation."
This is a time-tested playbook, though many a sharp market pullback has ended without what would qualify as unqualified capitulation.
The market action is winning some plaudits for the way non-tech stocks have held up better, many groups benefiting from the "quality" rotation while abandoned consumer cyclicals get a reprieve from easing oil prices and the slide in the 10-year Treasury yield back below 5%.
This gives active managers plenty to do in playing against a highly concentrated and tech-dependent S&P 500. But I'll continue to argue that the bull market built on the AI story will almost surely need the AI story to get back on track to keep advancing. A prolonged period when the equal-weight S&P 500 outperforms the market-cap-weighted version is otherwise known – usually – as a bear market.
The AI-related stocks' weighting in the S&P 500 is off the highs but remains near 45%, according to Morgan Stanley.
As the chart shows, AI has wobbled relative to the rest of the market during this uptrend before reasserting itself.  But there's a trickier element to the current gut check: In prior phases of the buildout, the key limiting bottleneck gave investors something to buy in order to exploit it.
The initial scarcity of GPUs meant to own Nvidia above all else from 2023 through 2024. When cloud capacity, power and cooling were found to be the crucial scarce resources, hyperscaler stocks worked and the AI-adjacent industrials were drastically revalued. Then memory emerged as the chokepoint and Micron and Sandisk went stratospheric.
Now, as Nvidia's Jensen Huang has said, capital is the constraint and that not only leaves no asset to buy, but it raises the cost of capital broadly as the mega-caps go free-cash-flow-negative.
Overlapping feedback loops and scrambled correlations across the markets and the real economy have further sapped investor conviction. Treasury yields no longer move with oil but largely with AI-capex sentiment, with both in retreat lately. AI-stock setbacks also mute inflation momentum and the equity wealth effect, meaning fewer Federal Reserve rate hikes are anticipated now versus a month ago.
This all probably sounds like an elaborate trap, and it has become one for the previously crowded trades. Could this reflect the end game for the AI-exuberance market chapter, which as I keep pointing out peaked around the SpaceX IPO in June? Impossible to say for sure, but if it were, I'm not sure things would look much different to this point.
But I don't want to dismiss the possibility that a lot of the known challenges are largely reflected in prices.
I argued in August that we should assume the valuation peak for this cycle was in. We've now retrenched to a forward P/E of 18.5 on the S&P 500 from 23 a year ago and the Nasdaq-100 at 20x is at the slimmest premium to the S&P 500 valuation in nine years. I'm on board with the idea that the market is telling us companies are now "over-earning," but if nothing else there is less valuation risk now than in recent months.
Sentiment toward AI stocks is in the dumps. Funds' positioning in tech has retreated below neutral. Important trading lows this year have happened near the turn of the month on March 30 and July 29, and the Nasdaq-100's relative-strength reading is exactly as oversold as it was at those turns.
So, stay alert for possible relief bounces that could evolve into something more consequential if indeed the midterm elections pass in a way that allows traders to unclench a bit into the year's home stretch.
John Kolovos of Macro Risk Advisors on the latest reading: "Similar to valuation, sentiment is not a timing tool, but it is getting harder and harder to find any bulls, as a near-perfect storm of tight financial conditions is being met with tech earnings that have gone from bad to worse in the blink of an eye."
-Another good big-picture conversation on the practical business and investment implications of the next phase of AI proliferation on Patrick O'Shaughnessy's Invest Like the Best podcast , this one with investor Cliff Sosin. His comparison of AI infrastructure economics to internet connectivity providers and his argument for how most of the productivity boost will go toward "consumer surplus" rather than corporate profits are particularly interesting.
-For my birthday Monday, my colleague and friend Sara Eisen wondered how I would write a birthday message to myself. I immediately regretted suggesting she ask ChatGPT, which generated this credible and somewhat embarrassing result :
"Another year older, though the longer-term trend remains constructive. Some modest deterioration in the underlying internals, perhaps, but nothing that suggests a decisive breakdown.
"The candles on the cake are approaching historically elevated levels, though valuation concerns have persisted for years without derailing the advance. At this stage, the key question isn't whether I've gotten older — that's largely priced in — but whether the wisdom gains can continue to offset the inevitable compression in energy multiples.
"For now, I'm maintaining a cautiously optimistic outlook, with upside optionality, downside support from family and friends, and no immediate need for Fed intervention. Happy birthday to me. The secular bull market remains intact."

articles.title_orig: 'Apparently I am afraid of heights': The Peruvian hotel with a terrifying check-in
articles.title_zh: 'Apparently I am afraid of heights': The Peruvian hotel with a terrifying check-in
articles.content_orig:
Suspended 365m above Peru's Sacred Valley, Skylodge's transparent sleeping pods offer extraordinary views – but getting there requires nerves of steel.
My legs quivered as I carefully repositioned my hiking boot on the half-inch braided wire beneath me. Gripping the via ferrata cable near my eyeline, I slipped my carabiner onto the next stretch of metal and took a step out over 200m (656ft) of free air.
"Apparently I am afraid of heights," I shouted behind me to my husband as he too navigated the precarious bridge. With only the cable beneath my feet, the sheer granite cliffs of Peru's Sacred Valley dropped away towards the murky-green Urubamba River far below. I shuffled awkwardly across the 20m (66ft) gap, repeating one instruction to myself: don't look down.
Finally at the other side, I eased myself onto a metal ladder. Our guide, Efren Lopez, assured me we had only a few hundred more metres to climb.
All this was simply the check-in process.
Our destination was Skylodge Adventure Suites , a collection of transparent capsules clinging to a sheer cliff face 365m (1,200ft) above the Sacred Valley floor – navigated via an expertly engineered series of ladders, wire traverses, iron rungs and steps. My husband and I, along with four others, had come to spend a night suspended above the Peruvian Andes.
Once the agricultural heartland of the Inca Empire, Peru's Sacred Valley draws visitors to its Inca ruins, traditional villages and spectacular mountain scenery. The small village of Pachar, where Skylodge is located, is just 10km (6.2 miles) away from the bustling Inca town of Ollantaytambo, but its fertile green floodplains and snow-capped Andean peaks feel worlds away.
Getting there: Skylodge Adventure Suites is approximately 90 minutes from Cusco. Guests reach the capsules via a guided two-hour via ferrata climb and descend via zipline.
How long: Choose between a half-day experience with lunch or a single-night stay.
How much: A one-night stay, including transfers from Cusco, guiding, the via ferrata ascent and zipline descent costs 1,640 Peruvian soles (£350/$480) per person
When to go: The dry season, typically April to October, for prime stargazing.
An easier alternative: The same operator also runs Starlodge Adventure Suites, lower on the cliffside and accessible via a short walk. Its capsules have showers, flushing toilets and an outdoor hot tub for star-gazing soaks.
Lopez led us steadily upwards, negotiating a series of narrow ledges carved into the granite cliff. Pausing on a small platform, barely wide enough for three people, I tightened my safety harness and looked out onto the valley. Far below, the Urubamba River twisted between cultivated fields, framed by sharp peaks.
Still dizzy, I dared to look towards the pods high above. As another climber struggled to squeeze onto the platform, I was nudged onward up the granite cliffside.
Despite my initial trepidation, I gradually found my rhythm, clipping and unclipping the carabiners as we climbed. But the thin mountain air left me wheezing as we crested 3,200m (10,500ft) above sea level, and by the time I finally hauled myself onto the metal platform outside the dining pod, two hours after beginning our ascent, I was exhausted.
Even here, there was little respite for anyone afraid of heights. The capsules seemed to hang over empty space. Only once I was safely inside, free of my harness, could I finally collapse into a chair and breathe.
My husband and I sat with our four climbing companions over a pot of tea, watching the sun set over the Sacred Valley through the dining pod's transparent walls, while our guide, Lopez, prepared a four-course Peruvian dinner. We tucked into pumpkin soup, chicken remoulade and Andean potatoes, followed by a rich cacao brownie topped with fresh maracuyá (passionfruit). Outside, the pink sky gradually darkened, revealing the first stars and the turbid spray of the Milky Way.
I downed the remainder of my wine in a single gulp as I remembered that reaching our bedroom would require another climb.
Lopez helped us back into our harnesses and clipped us in for the short ascent to our private pods. Using iron hand- and foot-grips drilled into the granite, my husband and I climbed towards our bedroom, where we'd remain until morning.
"Be sure to stay up late for the best views of the Milky Way," he reminded us.
Clinging to the cliff face, our sleeping pod was reached through a hatch in the roof. Inside were three beds – a double and two singles – and six windows offering views across the Sacred Valley. The bathroom was decidedly less luxurious: an ecologically friendly "dry" toilet, separated from the rest of the pod by a thick curtain, with no shower in sight.
• No cars, no phone signal: Canada's ghost island where guests still check in
• An icy 4,554m hike to Europe's highest overnight stay
• A stay in Pakistan's remote Ishkoman Valley, where humans still consult fairies
The temperature dropped quickly inside the pod and I curled up on the double bed beneath a pile of thick blankets, peering through the curved wall. There was little to do but read, sip wine and wait for the darkest hour and brightest stars. I listened to the faint sounds of civilisation drifting up the mountain from the road below: the occasional car horn, a distant siren and the rattle of wind whipping against the pod's exterior.
Earlier that evening, Lopez had explained the importance of the night sky in Inca culture. "The Urubamba River below us was viewed by the Incas as the earthly mirror of the Milky Way, and every living being had a celestial counterpart in the picturesque galaxy," he told us.
Now, lying high above the valley, I gazed up at the Milky Way while its earthly counterpart wound through the valley below. As the sky erupted with even more stars, I felt as though I was drifting to sleep among them, not beneath them.
Just before 06:00, golden morning light flooded my pod. Outside, birdsong echoed across the valley as the other guests began to stir.
After scuttling our way back to the dining pod for breakfast, we prepared for our final adventure: a descent along six ziplines, ranging from 150m (490ft) to 700m (2,300ft) in length. Clipping into the first line with confidence, I stole one last glance at the rugged hillside. I had finally found my sea legs up here.
Pushing off the platform, I hurtled between orange granite spires towards Lopez, who was waiting in the distance. Just before reaching the end of the line, I leaned right, avoiding a sharp whack as the automatic brake caught, helping me to drift lightly onto the next landing.
I careened from platform to platform, zig zagging down the cliff, lowering myself closer to the valley floor with each slide. Less than an hour later, I was back on solid ground.
The experience had been more challenging than any of us had imagined. But after a night suspended above the Sacred Valley, the quiet of nature, the deep satisfaction of enduring a physical challenge and the spectacular views had me fantasising about a future filled with climbs and cliffside camps.

articles.title_orig: What are the planned changes to immigration rules?
articles.title_zh: What are the planned changes to immigration rules?
articles.content_orig:
Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood has set out plans to overhaul immigration rules.
Proposals for stricter requirements to qualify for permanent settlement in the UK were first outlined in detail in November 2025, when Mahmood was home secretary in Sir Keir Starmer's government.
She has argued that settlement should be "earned", rather than being granted automatically, with those who contribute more to the country able to settle fastest.
Following a consultation , Mahmood has now announced her final decision on what changes should be taken forward.
Elements of her original proposals have been revised following a backlash from some Labour MPs, with plans to make foreign care workers already in the UK wait 15 years to qualify for settlement scrapped.
Indefinite leave to remain (ILR) – also known as settlement – gives someone the right to live, work and study in the UK for as long as they like.
Under the current system, people with ILR can also apply for benefits if they are eligible.
People who have lived in the UK for 12 months after being given ILR can apply for British citizenship, if they also meet other requirements .
Under the government's plans, the standard length of time migrants will have to live in the UK to qualify for permanent settlement will double from five to 10 years.
Under this 10-year pathway, applicants must have earned at least £12,571 for five of the seven years immediately before being granted settlement.
However, there will be a shorter qualifying period of five years for certain groups, including:
People earning over £125,141 a year, as well as "highly skilled" migrants such as those on Global Talent or Innovator Founder visas, will qualify after three years.
Migrants who have claimed certain benefits or breached immigration rules will only be able to settle after at least 20 years.
Adults with a criminal record will be refused settlement, with discretion to refuse cases where the offence was committed when the applicant was under 18.
To qualify for settlement, migrants will generally also have to meet other conditions, including:
There will be a different set of rules for refugees – people who have been granted asylum in the UK because they are unable to return to their own country as they fear persecution.
Refugees who arrived in the UK through an official government scheme will qualify for settlement after five years.
However, other refugees will need to wait 10 years and either work or study.
Those who do not work or study will need to wait 20 years.
Refugees who arrived in the UK by small boat or another illegal route will have to wait 20 years if they work or study, and 30 years if they don't.
The changes will apply to migrants who are already in the UK but not those who have already been granted settlement.
A partner who arrives with someone who then applies for ILR will be able to settle at the same time, as long as they meet the relevant requirements.
However, a partner who joins later will need to complete the same qualifying residence period before they are eligible for settlement.
Eligible couples will be able to combine their earnings to meet the minimum income  requirement.
The household income threshold will be £25,142 – twice the individual minimum income requirement.
Children under 18 will continue to be able to settle with their parents.
They will be exempt from the income, government debt, English language and Life in the UK test requirements, but will remain subject to the relevant suitability and criminality requirements.
Young adults aged 18 to 24, who remain dependant on their family, will also continue to be able to settle alongside them.
They will be expected to meet all the adult mandatory requirements but not the individual income requirement.
Someone who is aged 25 or over when their family becomes eligible for settlement will be expected to qualify independently.
Eligible partners, parents and children of British citizens will continue to qualify for settlement after five years.

articles.title_orig: Apple CEO John Ternus criticized for ‘scripted’ approach to first earnings call
articles.title_zh: Apple CEO John Ternus criticized for ‘scripted’ approach to first earnings call
articles.content_orig:
Investors didn’t seem overly happy about yesterday’s Apple earnings call despite the record results . That likely reflects the company’s cautious take on margins in the current quarter, but some have also criticized what they describe as a very “scripted” approach by new CEO John Ternus .
Bloomberg was the biggest critic, describing it as a “timid” performance that left analysts “sorely disappointed” …
Bloomberg’s Dave Lee didn’t hold back.
Apple investors and fans hoping to get an insight into the philosophy of new Chief Executive Officer John Ternus on Monday were left sorely disappointed. The 51-year-old’s first earnings call was a timid affair, with Ternus taking cover behind a carefully written script as analysts peppered him with questions.
Newly minted CEO plays it safe during his first high-stakes earnings call? Absolutely shocking! Seriously, what did Bloomberg expect?
Lee acknowledged that the slump in pre-market trading will have been largely driven by Apple’s caution about rising expenses in the current quarter. The company said that memory costs were continuing to rise and that building out Siri AI data centers we’re going to add to the RAM bill. But he argued that Ternus missed an opportunity to talk up the company.
In front of Ternus on Monday night was a chance to counteract the gloom and doom by instilling in Wall Street the fundamentals of the Ternus Doctrine — what he sees Apple becoming under his tenure, the “product guy” taking the company to a new era of innovation. Instead, he spoke like a man glancing at the clock and wishing the minutes away.
Fortune’s Sebastian Herrera was less vocal but echoed some of the criticism.
Ternus fielded some questions but also delegated answers to Chief Financial Officer Kevan Parekh and Chief Operating Officer Sabih Khan, who Apple said would participate in earnings calls moving forward, something the company hasn’t done for years. Ternus projected confidence on the call, but he appeared to stick mostly to scripted marketing points.
It will of course take Ternus some time to develop his own style when it comes to all of the varied aspects of the role, including addressing analysts in earnings calls, but I thought he took a measured but optimistic approach. Given the famously reticent style of his predecessor, the criticism strikes me as rather odd.
