articles.title_orig: King to open Commonwealth summit as Burnham begins talks on slavery apology
articles.title_zh: King to open Commonwealth summit as Burnham begins talks on slavery apology
articles.content_orig:
King Charles addresses the slave trade in a speech to Commonwealth leaders, saying the "shameful chapter of history is one that fills my heart with horror"
He was formally opening the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (Chogm) in Antigua and Barbuda
The powerful words from the King were careful and considered, and he spoke personally which will have landed with leaders - but he stopped short of a direct apology, our senior royal correspondent writes
The King also outlines what he describes as the "crisis of our time" , citing "brutal conflicts" facing the world, the "catastrophic reality" of climate change and the "dizzying speed" at which technology is transforming societies
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham is also at the summit, saying he is "open" to a formal apology from the UK over slavery, but said reparations were "not the right answer"
As part of talks with fellow leaders, Burnham is expected to set out plans for a "debt reset" to support Commonwealth countries dealing with the growing cost of paying interest
The Commonwealth leaders' summit is held every two years and allows leaders and representatives of the 56 nations to discuss the future of the partnership
Edited by Matt Spivey, with senior royal correspondent Daniela Relph and political editor Chris Mason in Antigua
Daniela Relph Senior royal correspondent, in Antigua
The words, as ever from the King, were careful and considered. But he spoke personally and that will have landed in a room full of leaders - many of whom want more from the UK.
There was no direct apology or offer of reparations but there was a sense of sorrow and contrition from the King in his own words.
There was an acknowledgement that he had personally learnt more about the brutality of the slave trade.
But there was also a sense from the King that the most powerful way forward is to look to the future and ensure the next generation of young people in the Commonwealth have the best opportunities made available to them.
âEvil need not have the last word,â the King said.
Joe Coughlan Live reporter
King Charles III has described the transatlantic slave trade as a "shameful chapter of history", adding that the period still casts a "shadow" over the Caribbean and wider Commonwealth.
Here's a recap of what he told the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting:
Concluding his speech, the King says he has only had time in this speech to mention "some of the ways" in which the Commonwealth is able to use its "unique advantage" to deliver tangible change.
Addressing the gathered leaders, he says the leadership of the Commonwealth is "in your hands".
"Each of you has the opportunity to make the greatest possible difference, I pray that over the coming days you will embrace this opportunity and commit yourselves to action," he says.
Above all, he says he trusts that each of the gathered leaders will commit to a Commonwealth in which "our young people can look to the future with greater confidence and purpose".
He ends by saying that he hopes people can draw inspiration from "this remarkable family of nations" as he himself has "always done".
The King mentions "brutal conflicts" the world is facing, and calls climate change a "catastrophic reality", which is leaving nature under constant attack.
He also says technology is transforming societies and economies "at dizzying speed", with little certainty about where it will lead us.
Together, these challenges "comprise the crisis of our time," the King continues.
The King then says that while the Commonwealth can't provide all of the solutions required, it does provide the opportunity to work together.
The monarch says the theme of this Chogm, accelerating partnerships and investment for a prosperous Commonwealth, represents a "vital opportunity" for us all.
On climate change, he adds that large ocean states have contributed little to the effects of climate change but are among those carrying the "greatest cost".
He says he is looking forward to hearing how Commonwealth leaders work with others such as the private sector on innovative proposals to tackle climate change.
Daniela Relph Senior royal correspondent, in Antigua
These are some of the most powerful words the King has ever said on the slave trade.
He addressed the UK role in the slave trade early on in the speech and spoke personally of his own horror and profound personal sorrow.
The King continues, saying that the more he has furthered his "understanding of the issues" the more committed he has become to "address the wrongs of the past with action for the future".
This includes, he says, improving access to education, investing in jobs and opportunities, encouraging "inter-Commonwealth trade" and tackling climate change.
"I have always felt there is so much that can be done to help lift up those who struggle against hardship," he says, adding that he has "always tried to play my part in doing just that".
He says the Commonwealth today is not just a product of the past, but a "response of the world of today", adding that "its vocation is more compelling than ever... in a desperately troubled world".
The King continues by saying the prism of time can be "both clarifying and distorting", but its consequences "resonate with contemporary force".
He says: "Our history inspires us, can appal us yet it can always teach us."
The monarch says the transatlantic trade in enslaved persons "still cast a shadow" over the Caribbean islands and other members of the Commonwealth.
"As I've said before, that shameful chapter of history is one that fills my heart with horror and my soul with the most profound personal sorrow," the King says.
He adds that character and courage can combine to overcome the "most monstrous injustice" as it did with the determination to end the international slave trade.
King Charles then pays tribute to the diversity of the Commonwealth, which he says has "mattered greatly" to him throughout his life.
None of us would be here today if not for our history, he continues, and says this history "is not ours to choose or change".
Our inheritance includes both our forebears' achievements and failures, he adds.
King Charles begins by saying he and the Queen are "delighted" to attend the 28th Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (Chogm), and adds it is "sobering" to think that he attended the first one 30 years ago.
He thanks the government of Antigua and Barbuda for their "remarkable hospitality".
"For one of the smallest nations on earth, your impact in the world is tremendous, and I think there is great truth is the saying 'small island, big vibes'," he says.
King Charles on stage at the Commonwealth summit in Antigua.
King Charles III is now standing on stage to deliver his speech at the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (Chogm) in Antigua.
We will be bringing you updates here and you can watch the speech live at the top of this page.
Commonwealth Secretary-General Shirley Botchwey describes the Commonwealth as an "indispensable agent of change" in a "world of rupture and uncertainty".
"Citizens from St John's to Sydney, Manchester to Mombasa are living through profound uncertainty," she says.
She says the goal of the summit is to "build a new model of partnership" capable of responding to the "scale of challenges we face".
She adds that too many Commonwealth nations are "held back by the rules on debt treatments" and says Commonwealth nations are working together to "change the international financial system".
The prime minister of host nation Antigua and Barbuda is first to speak on stage at the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (Chogm).
Gaston Browne says hosting the meeting is "more than a privilege" and tells the King: "We are deeply honoured by your presence as Head of the Commonwealth, together with her Majesty the Queen."
He adds at the last Chogm, in Samoa in 2024, nations agreed the time had come for a "truthful respectful conversation on reparatory justice".

articles.title_orig: Bonus PS Plus Premium Game Is Out Now for PS5
articles.title_zh: Bonus PS Plus Premium Game Is Out Now for PS5
articles.content_orig:
After a slight delay, PlayStation Plus users can now enjoy new-gen upgrades for two beloved Metro entries.
PlayStation Plus has gained a midweek treat for those who are subscribed to the premium tier.
After confusion as to whether they’d be available, free new-gen updates for Metro 2033 Redux and Metro Last Light Redux have now landed on the priciest tier, as spotted by Reddit user kabirsingh84 .
The new-gen updates first launched on consoles on October 29, but neither surfaced on PlayStation Plus with many wondering whether they were exclusive only to true owners of Metro 2033 Redux and Metro Last Light Redux.
Thankfully, it looks as if the rollout was instead just running a tad behind schedule with premium users now able to jump into the updated new-gen versions of both games.
Metro 2033 Redux and Metro Last Light Redux were already included exclusively on the premium tier; it’s not as if the new-gen upgrades have bumped them up from extra.
The two FPS titles, developed by 4A Games, originally landed on the premium tier back in September under the title Metro Redux which bundles 2033 Redux and Last Light Redux together.
As for what you can expect from the new-gen upgrades, 4A Games has finally introduced native PS5 and PS5 Pro support.
Both games also now offer up to 4K resolution at 60fps, with PSSR allowing for upscaled 4K at 120fps.
Textures have been improved, plus developers have made use of the DualSense controller’s adaptive triggers for a more immersive experience.
It’s slightly odd that Metro Redux is exclusive to the premium tier, which typically claims to offer a bonus ‘retro’ catalogue.
If you want PS1, PSP, PS2, and PS3 games, a premium subscription is perhaps the one for you.
If you just prefer PS4 and PS5 games, though, the extra tier is your best bet, or at least it was.
Metro 2033 first landed in 2010 on the PlayStation 4 with Last Light landing on the same console in 2013.
Why Metro Redux is reserved exclusively for the classics catalogue then, I don’t know.
READ MORE: PlayStation Plus drops 100-hour Final Fantasy rival RPG at no additional cost
As for what else you can get on the extra and premium tier as of late, October’s line-up has completed its rollout.
Extra tier users can enjoy Mafia: The Old Country, Horizon Forbidden West, Mycopunk, Poppy Playtime: Chapter 2, The Midnight Walk, Tales of Arise - Beyond The Dawn Edition , and Monster Energy Supercross 25 - The Official Video Game.
Premium users additionally received Dino Crisis 2 and RollerCoaster Tycoon 3 Complete Edition.
Since then, November’s essential tier line-up has also been confirmed with Tomb Raider IV-VI Remastered, Dead Island 2, and Monster Train 2 all available to play from today, November 3.
The extra and premium tiers are next due an update on Wednesday November 11, with those games due to start going live from Tuesday, November 17.

articles.title_orig: Yum Brands earnings beat estimates, but cyclospora outbreak weighs on Taco Bell
articles.title_zh: Yum Brands earnings beat estimates, but cyclospora outbreak weighs on Taco Bell
articles.content_orig:
Yum Brands on Tuesday reported earnings that beat expectations, but a cyclospora outbreak linked to iceberg lettuce at Taco Bell weighed on the company's same-store sales growth.
However, Yum said Taco Bell, which the company considers a "growth engine" for its business, has since rebounded.
"Since the end of September, Taco Bell U.S. has been outpacing the [quick-service restaurant] industry on same-store sales growth," Yum CEO Chris Turner said in a statement.
Taco Bell's same-store sales are up about 1% so far in the fourth quarter, CFO Ranjith Roy said on the company's earnings conference call Tuesday. In the last four weeks ended Friday, same-store sales have risen 3% compared with the year-ago period.
Here's what the company reported compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:
Yum reported fiscal third-quarter net income of $1.62 billion, or $5.92 per share, up from $397 million, or $1.41 per share, a year earlier.
Excluding gains from its divestiture of Pizza Hut and other items, the restaurant company earned $1.56 per share.
Net sales rose 4% to $2.05 billion.
During the quarter, Yum completed its divestiture of Pizza Hut. It closed the sale of the pizza chain's business in mainland China to Yum China on Aug. 7 and sold the rest of Pizza Hut to LongRange Capital on Sept. 1. The company's third-quarter results include Pizza Hut up until those dates.
Excluding Pizza Hut, Yum's same-store sales were flat for the quarter as Taco Bell weighed on the company's overall results. Taco Bell's same-store sales declined by 4% as diners temporarily pulled back on visits due to the foodborne illness outbreak .
Yum executives previously said the weekend of July 18 saw the most severe impact to sales, but trends have improved since then.
Taco Bell's most loyal customers returned faster, Yum said, thanks in part to weekly Tuesday deals for loyalty program members after the cyclospora outbreak took over headlines.
Traffic from "medium" and "light" customers has bounced back to about 95% of prior levels, while visits from "heavy" users is back to normal, Roy said. To attract more casual diners, Taco Bell has been relying on star power, like a collaboration with pop star Olivia Rodrigo on a pink-colored Mountain Dew Baja Blast.
Outside of the U.S., Taco Bell's much smaller international business reported same-store sales growth of 5%.
KFC's same-store sales ticked up 1%, helped by system sales growth in China and Europe. The U.S., now the chicken chain's third-largest market, saw system sales shrink 6% in the quarter.
Like Restaurant Brands International's Popeyes , KFC has struggled in the U.S. amid a wave of new competitors and more budget-conscious consumers. Its home market represents only about 5% of KFC's operating profit, but it remains a symbolically important part of the business for Yum investors.
During the quarter, KFC U.S. launched popcorn chicken, which sold out in many restaurants. However, Yum said the limited-time menu item was not enough to offset the successful Hot & Spicy Wings and Potato Wedges promotion during the year-ago period.
Globally, KFC is trying to become "the most modern chicken QSR ," Turner said on the company's earnings conference call. To achieve that lofty goal, he said the chain will roll out buzzy promotions, a new brand identity, and a wider menu that includes upgraded sauces and more beverages.

articles.title_orig: University to revert to original name in merger
articles.title_zh: University to revert to original name in merger
articles.content_orig:
Cranfield University will revert to being known by its former name as part of a merger with King's College London.
The Bedfordshire institution will once again be the Cranfield Institute of Technology when the merger is completed next August. It has been known by its current name since 1993.
It will become the 10th faculty of King's and will include Cranfield Defence and Security, which will work with the King's School of Security Studies.
Prof Shitij Kapur, vice-chancellor and president of King's, said the merger was intended to "enhance the impact that King's and Cranfield already have on our society".
He said: "I'm confident that welcoming Cranfield with all its unique strengths, world class facilities and deep industry partnerships into our community will help us achieve that and support our Strategy 2030 to build a bigger, better King's."
The merger will involve Cranfield's School of Management joining King's Business School.
Before the agreement was signed, the only information the universities could exchange was that needed for due diligence. Detailed integration planning can now get under way.
Current Cranfield students and those who accept offers before the merger takes place can choose whether their degree certificates are issued by King's or Cranfield. Those accepting offers after the merger will receive King's certificates.
Prof Dame Karen Holford, chief executive and vice-chancellor of Cranfield University, said: "We now embark on a new chapter, joining our specialisms with King's world-class education, research and scale.
"Together, we'll build a nationally significant asset and a global university that will bring even more positive impacts to people's lives."

articles.title_zh: Midterm elections could jolt stocks if Democrats sweep Congress
articles.content_orig:
The stock market is not yet pricing in a Democratic sweep of Congress — despite some polls and most prediction markets pointing that way — so that scenario could weigh on share prices Wednesday, according to investors and analysts.
Republicans managing to keep control could cause a short-term relief rally, they said.
Short-term moves aside, the typical post-midterm pattern in the months ahead is bullish. But some wonder if the market could buck the positive historical trend this time because the S&P 500 is already up so much this year going into the election.
As far as certain stocks to watch, a big Democratic win on Tuesday night — especially in the Texas governor race — could add fuel to an AI stock sell-off on the notion that more data center restrictions would gain momentum nationally. Defense stocks could come under pressure on fears of limits on spending.
Polls are pointing to a Democratic victory in the House and a toss-up in the Senate. Prediction markets have been more favorable to Democrats, calling for a blue sweep .
While investors are signaling "begrudging acceptance" to a base case scenario that there will indeed be a Democratic sweep, that's not how they're positioning, said Tobin Marcus, head of U.S. policy and politics at Wolfe Research. The firm's recent survey data among more than 100 institutional investors suggests they are not strongly positioned for any particular result.
"Investors seem to have a significant dose of skepticism about whether the final outcome is going to be quite as favorable to Democrats as the polling suggests," Marcus told CNBC, noting that the firm shares the view that the "polling is likely overstating Democratic strength."
JPMorgan sees a blue wave knocking the S&P 500 by about a half percent on Wednesday.
On the other hand, if Republicans end up retaining both chambers of Congress, that could spur a rally, said Sameer Samana, head of global equities and real assets at Wells Fargo Investment Institute.
"From a certainty standpoint, the market knows what to do with Republicans holding both chambers," he said.
Citigroup strategists said Monday that Republicans losing the House but managing to keep the Senate could be "a tailwind for equities into year-end." JPMorgan traders predict up to a 1% pop on Wednesday if Republicans hold on to that chamber.
Looking past any short-term move, stocks tend to rally after the midterms have concluded. In fact, the S&P 500 was up one year out after all midterm elections going back to the early 1980s.
But the S&P 500 has already recorded double-digit gains so far in 2026, so some on Wall Street worry that investors are being overly complacent heading into this year's elections.
During midterm election years, the S&P 500 has typically averaged a 14% drawdown at some point in the second half of the year found Jonathan Krinsky, chief market technician at BTIG.
"The reason stocks often perform well in November during midterms is because [the S&P 500] typically is weak INTO the elections. We have the opposite setup this year," Krinsky wrote last week. "Therefore, while consensus is that we see a post midterm rally, we think the opposite is actually more likely."
It's not helping that the broader market has recently come under significant pressure due to turbulence in the AI trade, which led the Nasdaq Composite to post its worst day since June on Friday. AI shares led the market lower again on Monday.
A strong showing from Democrats in Tuesday's midterm elections could pressure the trade even more .
At the state level, increased Democratic control is probably a headwind for stocks associated with data centers and technological capital equipment, analysts said.
"It [would solidify] the early kind of cautionary signs in different states around the advancement of AI infrastructure," Rob Rains at Washington Analysis told CNBC.
Goldman Sachs strategists said this week that a Democratic Congress "might limit data center tax incentives, but a national moratorium looks unlikely in any election outcome."
One example would be Texas — a key hub of the data-center buildout. A surprise loss there by Republican Gov. Greg Abbott has the "potential to spook" the market in the short term, Wolfe's Marcus said.
A blue wave might pressure defense shares, while boosting health care stocks, analysts and investors said.
"A substantial Democratic sweep could limit real spending growth unless a broader agreement increases both defense and health-care funding," said Alex Sagal, global equity analyst at Wells Fargo Investment Institute. However, he noted that the earnings outlook for the defense industry looks "stable to modestly positive."
Wolfe Research's Marcus said that healthcare is going to be "the biggest focus," as Democrats will push for restoring expired Affordable Care Act enhanced premium subsidies or unwinding some of the Medicaid reforms in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act .
"Healthcare stocks have been doing really well lately," Jed Ellerbroek, portfolio manager at Argent Capital Management, said to CNBC. "I think part of that is the anti-AI trade, but I also think part of it is just optimism that Democrats are taking over."
Ellerbroek is keeping his eye on hospital-related stocks such as HCA Healthcare and Tenet Healthcare as well as health insurers like UnitedHealth and Centene .
Financials was the worst S&P 500 sector in early 2026 on the heels of President Donald Trump calling on Congress to pass a law that would cap credit card interest rates at 10% . While the sector has been able to notch gains since, with its year-to-date rise now at around 3%, things could get more unstable for the group under Democratic control.
"Democrats will come in wanting to show tangible progress on the affordability issue, and that means targeting sectors that are front and center in consumer budgets," said Evercore ISI's Matthew Aks. "We know Trump has populist instincts, populist leanings, and could he pick a couple of issues and decide to team up with the Democrats on those issues and target those industries in a populist way? Absolutely."
Given that Democratic control is often associated with increased regulation, while Republican control is thought to promote deregulation, Democrats could be interested in passing credit card rate caps if they come out victorious.
"I think if Democrats have control of one or both chambers, they would try to pass it and see if they could get Trump to either sign it or force him to veto it, and that would let Democrats kind of score a political point," Aks said.
Trump could restart the war against Iran after holding off any major strikes leading up to the midterms, a move that could upend the overall market and cause energy stocks to outperform. Crude oil prices jumped more than 10% in October, though they gave a lot of that gain back on Monday.
Gasoline prices stood at $4.17 a gallon on average nationwide Sunday, a nearly 40% increase compared to the same period last year, per AAA.
"If there are escalations, that could obviously put upward pressure on prices just ahead of Thanksgiving," said Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysts at Gas Buddy, "which is also when Americans have really staunch traditions in terms of driving to friends and family."
If Trump decides to take forceful action, it could snuff out hope for a typical post-midterm year-end rally.
Evercore ISI said the S&P 500 could retreat by double-digits to end the year at 6,800 as oil spikes if the president "moves to kinetic escalation in Iran ahead of seating the new Congress in January" and Democrats take Congress.
— With reporting by Sarah Min, Tobias Burns and Spencer Kimball

articles.title_orig: Palantir Stock Tumbles Even as Earnings Get Big Boost From U.S. Customers
articles.title_zh: Palantir Stock Tumbles Even as Earnings Get Big Boost From U.S. Customers
articles.content_orig:
Investors are hammering Palantir stock on Tuesday, dumping shares even after the AI-powered data software firm delivered strong third-quarter earnings.
Shares of the company fell as much as 7% to $165.25. Palantir beat Wall Street's estimates on key metrics in the quarter, and reported that commercial revenue exceeded revenue from government contracts for the first time. Total revenue of $2.31 billion blew past analysts' expectations.
However, a sharp slowdown in commercial bookings compared to the second quarter rattled investors' view of the stock. The firm reported year over year commercial bookings growth of 11%, compared to 153% booking growth in the prior quarter.
"Analysts blamed a deceleration in US commercial bookings for the selloff, which has taken the stock down to support around $165," David Morrison, senior market analyst at Trade Nation, said. "These are all indications that there's some fragility spreading across the AI-adjacent trade."
It's the latest example of a hiccup in an otherwise rosy earnings report derailing a high-flying tech stock. Palantir's move is emblematic of just how high investors' expectations have risen, to the point where shares sell off at the first sign of trouble.
Other tech giants know well already, with hyperscalers and other AI builders under intense scrutiny when it comes to things like capex spending , which can overshadow other bright spots in earnings reports.
The tech trade has also weakened broadly in recent weeks. Volatility throughout Asian markets , spanning China, Japan, and South Korea, has led to heightened concern that the AI bubble may be about to pop .
Luke Lango, chief technology analyst at InvestorPlace noted that while his team is still bullish on Palantir, the company doesn't just have to prove its doing well — it has to continuously justify its premium valuation.
"Palantir's rearview looks spectacular, while the view through the windshield got a little foggier after bookings cooled sharply from last quarter's record," Lango said. "For most stocks, that's a footnote. For a stock priced for perfection, it's the headline bears have been waiting for."
Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters.
Others have highlighted the threat that rising competition could pose, particularly as compute costs continue rising .
"Palantir's sequential deceleration in commercial customer additions, the slowest since 3Q24, suggests rising competition from frontier model providers," noted Bloomberg Intelligence analyst William Tong. "Gross margin declined roughly 100 bps in 3Q, suggesting higher compute requirements may remain a near-term headwind as inference-intensive workloads scale."
That said, bulls remain focused on Palantir's strong growth prospects. UBS analyst Karl Keirstead said the company's 96% revenue growth outweighs any negative aspects of the earnings report, and reiterated a Buy rating for the stock.
"The only real flaw in the print was the sequentially flat RPO/backlog (first time since 1Q23), which Palantir pinned mostly on shorter contract durations," Keirstead wrote.

articles.title_orig: Apple unsure when it will get more foldable iPhones ahead of Christmas
articles.title_zh: Apple unsure when it will get more foldable iPhones ahead of Christmas
articles.content_orig:
Apple has said it does not know when it will get more of its new foldable iPhones back in stock as the company heads towards the key Christmas trading period.
The iPhone Duo sold out just over a week after its launch, despite being Apple's most expensive smartphone at a cost of nearly $2,000.
The company warned of "constraints" in sourcing key components and admitted it was "really hard to predict when supply and demand will be in balance".
Meanwhile, Apple's new chief executive John Ternus said the firm was seeing an "unprecedented" price rise in memory costs, including chips, as the artificial intelligence (AI) industry continues to invest billions of dollars in building data centres.
Ternus launched the Duo after he took over from previous boss Tim Cook in September.
It is the smartphone's first major design change in almost 20 years but some buyers have reported problems with the Duo's screen .
Last week, the company said it would replace any handsets that were affected by an issue that caused a "small number" to crack along the inside fold.
As it released its latest financial figures on Monday, Apple's executives did not mention any problems with the iPhone Duo.
Ternus said he was "thrilled" by the early reaction to the foldable phone. Chief operating officer Sabih Khan said the company was working hard to get the Duo "into the hands of our customers as quickly as possible".
Apple's results for the three months to 26 September did not include sales of the Duo, which was released at the end of October.
Nevertheless, Apple said it had sold more iPhones globally over the last year than ever before.
iPhone revenue for the quarter rose 17% to $57bn (£42bn).
Sales of Mac computers also grew over the three months by 27% to a record $10.7bn.
Overall, Apple's sales between July and September rose from $102bn to $114bn. Pre-tax profit also increased, from $32.8bn to $36.1bn.
However, sales for both the iPad and Apple's wearable products, including its headphones and watch, fell by 10% and 7%, respectively.
Khan said that most Apple devices were still experiencing supply constraints driven in part by difficulty in getting enough microprocessors with advanced nodes.
Those components are essentially computer chip technology that allow Apple devices to operate more quickly, most of which it has manufactured through TSMC, which is based in Taiwan.
Khan said the problem was expected to continue into next year, particularly impacting iPads and Macs.
The situation has been made worse by what the company has repeatedly insisted is "unexpected demand" for its products.
Ternus noted, too, that Apple is still seeing "unprecedented" cost increases for memory, or the ability of devices to store data like apps, photos and text messages.
Much memory storage runs through data centres, which have experienced a boom in demand for space as AI chatbots and platforms - including those developed by the likes of OpenAI and Anthropic - have become popular.
Storage prices have gone up for tech companies like Apple.
Earlier this year, Cook referred to a sudden increase in data centre costs as a "thousand year flood".
Apple has lifted prices on nearly all of its hardware products by around 20%.
Sunil Krishnan from Aviva Investors told the BBC's Today programme that Apple posted "a reasonably solid set of results" with a "pretty good performance" from its iPhone business.
While there were concerns over the company's guidance on profit margins and the cost of memory chips, Krishnan added that in the broader context, "margins well north of 45% for a very well-established company, I think, are pretty impressive".
However, Apple's share price fell by 1.8% in after-hours trading.

articles.title_orig: Campaign to keep Ilhan Omar’s secrets safe includes threats against anyone who speaks out: ‘You’ll be killed … snake’
articles.title_zh: Campaign to keep Ilhan Omar’s secrets safe includes threats against anyone who speaks out: ‘You’ll be killed … snake’
articles.content_orig:
A 1-year-old girl was killed at a Sacramento cemetery on Sunday while visiting her grandmother’s gravesite with her family for Día de los Muertos — after allegedly being struck by a drunk driver.
The driver is now in custody on a manslaughter charge.
Miguel Guzman, 50, was arrested and booked into the Sacramento County Main Jail, according to police.
The biggest news, opinion and culture shaping California right now.
He faces several charges, including gross vehicular manslaughter while intoxicated and other DUI-related offenses.
Sacramento police responded to the crash near St. Mary Cemetery shortly before 5 p.m. Janessa Milagro Mazur Diaz, the 1-year-old girl, and her father were found injured at the scene.
The child later died from her injuries at the hospital, according to her family.
The child’s mother, Jackline Patino Diaz, told KCRA 3 that the family had recently celebrated Janessa’s first birthday.
“We were just celebrating, never in a bad mood,” she said.
Meanwhile, the child’s father, who was also injured in the crash, remains in the ICU with broken ribs, a fractured nose and skull.
Diaz told KCRA 3 about the heartbreaking moment she had to tell him their daughter had died.
“The first thing he asked me when I walked in the room was, ‘Where’s my baby?’ and I had to tell him she was gone,” she told the TV news station. “She’s not here with us anymore. It’s so crazy to think that we were just sitting at the cemetery, and he just came and ran over her, and now she’s gone. She’s not here with us.”
Guzman initially remained at the scene but allegedly attempted to leave before police detained him. Investigators are now looking into the crash as a hit-and-run.
The family has launched a GoFundMe to help cover Janessa’s funeral costs, her father’s medical expenses and other financial needs.
“We are heartbroken beyond words. No parent should ever have to experience the pain of losing their child,” the family wrote on the fundraising page. “Our sweet Janessa was taken from us far too soon, and we would give anything to have her back in our arms.”
As of Tuesday morning, the family had raised more than $19,000 toward its $35,000 goal.
“Any donation, no matter how small, would mean more than words can express,” the GoFundMe reads.
The family also shared an emotional tribute to Janessa.
“Our sweet Janessa Milagro, Mommy will love you forever. You deserved a lifetime of birthdays, laughter, hugs, and beautiful memories. Your little life made an impact that will never be forgotten.”
Guzman remains in custody with bail set at $470,000, according to jail records.
He is scheduled to appear in court Tuesday afternoon.

articles.title_orig: South of Midnight director says he wouldn’t have funded it if he was Xbox, and he knew ‘Rome would burn’ eventually
articles.title_zh: South of Midnight director says he wouldn’t have funded it if he was Xbox, and he knew ‘Rome would burn’ eventually
articles.content_orig:
We absolutely loved South of Midnight when it launched last year as an Xbox first-party title from Compulsion Games, and it's still one of our favourite Xbox Game Studios releases of recent years. However, a year later, Xbox has parted ways with the development team and helped transition them back to an independent studio.
In a nutshell, it seems Xbox wasn't happy enough with South of Midnight's performance from a revenue standpoint, and the same could be said for other smaller releases last year like Double Fine's Keeper and Kiln .
Some fans had been voicing their concerns prior to these releases that Xbox might be putting too much funding into them, and speaking on a recent podcast, South of Midnight director David Sears admitted that he was "always worried" that the funding situation might change and cause Xbox to "close the floodgates".
Here's an excerpt from the MinnMax podcast in which he said this:
"I mean, [Xbox] were funding a lot of games. They were also funding a lot of studios that, you know, I was like, well, okay, great. I guess you have infinite money. Like I was saying earlier, I don't want to feel the weight of the obligation of giant budget or an army of 600 to be responsible for. I want to make something that isn't going to bankrupt Microsoft, I guess, or the games division."
"So, you know, on one hand, if everyone you're working with is either trying to make generational games at not a huge expense, or games that have huge or really significant contemporary commercial appeal, great. It's going to work. But when does that ever happen?"
"I literally told people, 'Wow, this could be terrible.' Because somebody is going to say one day, 'We're closing those floodgates.' And that's going to have really traumatic results downstream."
Perhaps most shockingly, the director went on to admit that as much as he wanted to make South of Midnight, it perhaps wasn't sustainable from a funding perspective in hindsight, and that a "shocking outcome" seemed inevitable.
" I mean, I wanted to make it. No doubt, and obviously, because we made it. Would I have turned off someone else's money flow before South of Midnight? Yeah, 'cause I'm not completely selfless. But it just seems like, in hindsight at least, it was unsustainable. So, of course it was going to have a shocking outcome."
"I mean, it's easy to dissect it now. At the time, I would talk to other directors and would be like, 'How is this happening? How did we get so lucky? Is this a golden era?' And I would always be like, 'For now, right? There's always a night when Rome burns.' And I didn't know exactly when it would be, but I was always worried about it."
Of course, none of this is to suggest that Sears wasn't proud of South of Midnight, or that he didn't think it was worthwhile, but it just appears he was concerned with the Xbox money was putting into (and expecting back) for it.
Nevertheless, it seems like he had a very positive experience working with Microsoft overall:
"To their credit, it's amazing, right? I think there's definitely corporate Microsoft DNA but they're vastly different from the Microsoft I knew back in the '90s or the early 2000s, right? Much more humane, actually. It's remarkable and commendable."
"Working on South of Midnight, it became clear to me - some games, their time is not on release. Some games are generational, right? Something that has a good message or is transportive to places that will remain timeless will endure and audiences will find them."
His prediction did ultimately come true - Xbox decided to "close the floodgates" earlier this year by splitting from multiple studios including Compulsion Games, and seemingly adopting a new strategy of focusing on their core franchises like Halo , Forza , Gears , Fallout and others.
We're just pleased that Compulsion Games didn't end up getting closed altogether, and that South of Midnight did actually see the light of day instead of being cancelled during development. We reckon it could end up being one of those Sunset Overdrive -style titles in the future - a cult classic that people end up really enjoying from years past.

articles.title_orig: Smugglers Bypass U.S. Controls to Ship HBM to China
articles.title_zh: Smugglers Bypass U.S. Controls to Ship HBM to China
articles.content_orig:
Despite U.S. export controls on advanced semiconductors to China, High Bandwidth Memory (HBM) produced by Samsung Electronics and SK hynix is reportedly being smuggled into China. Smugglers are using a method of packaging HBMs with low-end server processors to bypass export regulations, and then detaching only the memory once in China.
According to the U.S. IT media outlet The Information on Nov. 2 (local time), smugglers who have recently been siphoning Korean HBMs to China are exploiting loopholes in export regulations.
They package the HBM with a low-end server processor on a board and export it to China. They target the fact that while exporting HBM alone is subject to U.S. regulations, packaging it with a server processor classifies the package as a server processor item.
Under U.S. export regulations, the total computing power of a semiconductor package is evaluated based on the server processor, not the memory chip. The packages are disassembled upon arriving in China. Local technicians apply heat to the board to melt the solder, detach only the necessary HBM, and discard the remaining server processors.
The separation process requires highly sophisticated skills. It is reported that the failure rate is high because applying heat too quickly or for an extended period can cause the memory stack to warp or crack.
Nevertheless, the smuggling continues due to the massive profits.
A broker in his 20s who handles HBM smuggling in China told The Information that the price of a single HBM3E, which traded for several hundred dollars just a year ago, has recently soared to about $4,000. A single AI chip package requires 6 to 8 HBMs. The memory price alone amounts to $24,000 to $32,000. AI processors, servers, and power costs are separate.
The HBMs secured in this way are reportedly sold mainly to customers of Huawei, a Chinese telecommunications equipment and IT company.
According to sources familiar with Huawei’s supply chain, Huawei recently explained to some customers that its next-generation flagship AI chip, the Ascend 960DT, will largely be equipped with HBMs produced by Samsung Electronics and SK hynix. Huawei introduced that the performance of the Ascend 960DT is twice as superior as existing chips, and it will be one of the powerful processors that China can produce on its own.
As it became difficult to directly purchase the necessary memory chips from Korean companies, Huawei even advised some AI chip ordering customers to secure HBMs on their own. China is clinging to securing Korean HBMs because it lacks its own production capacity.
HBM is a core component that enhances the processing performance of AI processors by quickly transmitting large amounts of data. Without securing enough HBMs, it is difficult for a high-performance AI chip to exert its full performance even if it is developed. Samsung Electronics and SK hynix account for more than 80% of the global HBM market.
The problem is that such smuggling could also act as a burden on Korean semiconductor companies. Even if Samsung Electronics and SK hynix did not directly violate export control regulations, they could become targets of U.S. government surveillance if Chinese AI chips equipped with their memory are discovered.
In fact, Taiwan’s TSMC was investigated by the U.S. government in 2024 after semiconductors it produced were found in Huawei products. Subsequently, the U.S. ordered TSMC to completely halt AI chip exports to China.
SK hynix stated, “We are strictly complying with relevant laws and regulations, including the export control regulations of the U.S. and South Korea,” adding that it has never supplied products to Huawei since the implementation of U.S. export regulations in 2020.
Meanwhile, a perception is emerging among smugglers who consider their transactions to be a patriotic act.
A broker in his 20s who smuggles memory in China told The Information regarding his work, “It is contributing to the motherland.” He reportedly does not consider himself a smuggler.
However, as smuggling competition intensifies, concerns about crackdowns are also growing.
Another smuggler who has been ordering memory semiconductors from South Korea revealed that the risk of detection is increasing as other brokers have started using the transaction routes he used.
He said, “The more people like us there are, the easier it becomes to be discovered by regulatory authorities,” adding that he plans to sell most of his company stakes next year as crackdowns by South Korea and the U.S. are expected to be further strengthened in the future.

articles.title_orig: Labour MPs pull their punches on immigration changes
articles.title_zh: Labour MPs pull their punches on immigration changes
articles.content_orig:
Today's announcement has long been viewed in government as a potential political banana skin.
When the home secretary announced her first version of changes to the settlement system last year, many Labour MPs, including the housing secretary Angela Rayner, voiced their concerns about the plans.
But there was a feeling that Sir Keir Starmer's government was determined to plough on regardless. Shabana Mahmood herself repeatedly expressed how important she believed the reforms were.
But the change of prime minister over the summer gave renewed hope to those unhappy Labour MPs that they could force the Home Office into two changes.
Firstly, social care workers – under the original plans many social care workers would have had to wait 15 years before becoming eligible for settlement.
Secondly, the retrospective nature of the plans – some MPs were uncomfortable at the idea of someone coming to the UK and expecting to be eligible for settlement after five years, but then having to wait longer.
Angela Rayner described that as "un-British" and said the government shouldn't be shifting "the goalposts".
She returned to the cabinet under Andy Burnham as housing secretary and chose to repeat those criticisms in an interview during the Labour Party conference in September.
That was seen as evidence that a debate inside the top levels of government about whether to water down the plans was well and truly rumbling on.
For all the Labour MPs who wanted a change, there were others, particularly those in Brexit-supporting areas, who wanted the home secretary to stick the course.
Some inside government felt nervous about providing what they saw as catnip to Reform and the Conservatives.
All of that added up to one of the more difficult decisions that has had to be taken since Burnham walked through the doors of Number 10.
In the end ministers chose to water down the proposals for care workers – those who arrived before May 2025 and earn at least £25,000 a year will qualify for settlement in five years.
But the retrospective nature of the plans, the thing Rayner described as shifting "the goalposts", hasn't changed.
Despite that, the majority of Labour MPs pulled their punches when Mahmood made a statement in the House of Commons earlier .
Perhaps the strongest pushback came from Rachael Maskell, who is no fan of the retrospective element - but others on the left of the party, including John McDonnell and Diane Abbott, were critical without being scathing.
Outside the Commons chamber, the mood among Labour folk was pretty similar to what was said from the green benches.
One would-be critic said that while they personally still had concerns about the plans announced today, they believed the Home Secretary had successfully taken the political sting out of the situation for now.
They said the campaign by MPs and unions had led to a "big win" on settlement for social care workers, but said they were still expecting to hear from constituents negatively affected by the new rules.
One Number 10 source praised Mahmood's "take no prisoners" performance in the chamber, argued she had "found the right balance" and said the announcement had gone down as well as could be expected with Labour colleagues.
Of course, the home secretary will still need to deal with criticism from other parties.
Her opposite number for the Conservatives, Chris Philp, accused Mahmood of a significant U-turn.
Philp highlighted a claim she had previously made – that allowing care workers to reach settlement more quickly could cost the UK £10bn.
The social care workers plans announced today will see around 500,000 people have their path to settlement delayed , that number would have been around 800,000 under the original plans last year.
In an interview with the BBC, Mahmood wouldn't say what sort of financial burden her watering down would result in.
She also refused to confirm whether Burnham had directly asked her to water down the plans.
They are tricky questions that she will have to navigate over the coming weeks.
But the general view within government is that this is one political hurdle that has been successfully jumped.

articles.title_orig: US, Russia and China discuss trilateral meeting between Trump, Putin and Xi
articles.title_zh: US, Russia and China discuss trilateral meeting between Trump, Putin and Xi
articles.content_orig:
Fox News chief foreign correspondent Trey Yingst reports on Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's response to Russian attacks, warning that strikes on their infrastructure will meet a painful response.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned Monday that Russia is preparing a "massive attack" on Ukraine centered on Tuesday's midterm elections in the United States, accusing Moscow of seeking to exploit the historical vote to unleash strikes while the world's attention is elsewhere.
The Ukrainian leader's warning came as voters prepared to decide which party controls Congress, a result that could also influence Washington's future response to Russian President Vladimir Putin's almost five-year war in Ukraine.
In a post on X, Zelenskyy went on to urge the Trump administration to increase pressure on Moscow, warning that Russia could exploit the elections to target Ukraine's battered energy infrastructure and supply routes.
DRONE STRIKE SINKS SHIP IN NATO WATERS AS ZELENSKYY WARNS OF LOOMING ‘MASSIVE STRIKE’
Russian President Vladimir Putin and Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. (Vyacheslav Prokofyev/Sputnik/Kremlin Pool Photo/Efrem Lukatsky/AP)
"We have intel that Russia is preparing a new massive attack on our country – primarily targeting energy and logistics," Zelenskyy said in his nightly address.
"The assumption is basically that tomorrow the world will be watching the American midterms, and what is happening here in Ukraine, along with our difficulties with air defense and Patriot missiles, will be overlooked."
Zelenskyy's warning came hours after Russian forces struck a school being used to distribute humanitarian aid in Komyshuvakha, a settlement in southeastern Ukraine's Zaporizhzhia region.
At least 26 people, including police officers and first responders, were killed, five others were injured and others remained missing, according to the Ukrainian news outlet Ukrainska Pravda .
ZELENSKYY PRESSURES US AND EUROPE FOR MORE 'AIR DEFENSE' ASSISTANCE AMID ONGOING WAR WITH RUSSIA
Ukraine's largest private energy company reports 90% of generation capacity damaged by Russian attacks, leaving over 1 million without power during freezing temperatures. (Reuters)
In his X post, Zelenskyy urged the U.S. and its allies to warn Putin that continued attacks on Ukraine would bring serious economic consequences.
"We need signals from the world to Russia that will make them feel that terror is no good, that it will bring no gains, and that as long as this war continues, their oil will burn, and they will not be able to make money doing business with the world," Zelenskyy warned.
"We must not play games with Russia's oil or gas revenues," he added.
"We must put pressure on Russia in such a way that it has no alternative but to end this war. America can do this."
TRUMP ANNOUNCES IMMEDIATE ENERGY CEASEFIRE BETWEEN RUSSIA AND UKRAINE
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, left talks with President Donald Trump and members of his Cabinet during a lunch meeting at the White House on Oct. 17, 2025, in Washington, D.C. (Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)
President Donald Trump, meanwhile, has sought to negotiate an end to the war with the help of special envoy Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner , both of whom have been involved in diplomatic efforts with Moscow.
Zelenskyy told Fox News in a Sunday interview that Ukraine would suspend strikes on Russian oil refineries for a month if Washington provided Patriot missile interceptors during the same period, potentially opening the door to diplomacy.
The State Department approved the potential sale of 500 Patriot PAC-3 interceptor missiles to Ukraine for an estimated $2.1 billion, according to Reuters.
The proposed sale could provide a significant boost to Ukraine's air defenses if finalized, although the delivery timeline is uncertain.
TRUMP SAYS US WILL LET UKRAINE MAKE PATRIOT MISSILES IN MAJOR POLICY SHIFT
First Lady Melania Trump, left, and civilians being evacuated from Oleshky, Ukraine, in October 2022 during the early days of the Russia-Ukraine war. (Umit Bektas/Reuters; Alexander Ermochenko/Reuters)
On Monday, Ukraine also accused Moscow of exploiting a U.S.-backed humanitarian ceasefire in Oleshky , in Ukraine's southern Kherson region, to strengthen Russian military positions.
Nearly 800 people were evacuated during the six-day humanitarian pause, according to first lady Melania Trump, with the White House clarifying that she helped broker the arrangement.
Ukraine's General Staff accused Russian forces of using the humanitarian pause to rotate troops, reinforce their defenses and improve battlefield logistics.
"Under the ceasefire introduced for the humanitarian operation in Oleshky, units of the Defence Forces of Ukraine ensured that the ceasefire was observed and acted exclusively within the framework of the agreements reached," the General Staff said in a statement on X.

"The enemy, by contrast, used the humanitarian pause to improve its positions."
Emma Bussey is a breaking news writer for Fox News Digital. Before joining Fox, she worked at The Telegraph with the U.S. overnight team, across desks including foreign, politics, news, sport and culture.

articles.title_zh: Single check-in for those in Hong Kong transit under scheme with mainland China
articles.content_orig:
Those travelling from Hangzhou or Wuhan can have bags checked through to final destination overseas under new one-stop service launched on Tuesday
Travellers flying from Hangzhou or Wuhan to overseas destinations via Hong Kong on different airlines can have their baggage checked through to the final destination under a newly launched service that aims to step up the connections between mainland Chinese cities and other countries.
Under the new one-stop service that launched on Tuesday, travellers departing from Hangzhou Xiaoshan International Airport or Wuhan Tianhe International Airport will not need to check in their baggage again when transferring through Hong Kong, even if they are flying on a different airline on the next leg of their journey.
“Hong Kong International Airport is launching a game-changing service,” Secretary for Transport and Logistics Mable Chan said.

articles.title_orig: Asian trading is mixed as tech sell-off deepens and oil prices rebound
articles.title_zh: Asian trading is mixed as tech sell-off deepens and oil prices rebound
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Oil prices tumbled more than seven percent on Monday, the eve of crucial midterm elections in the United States, as signals that Tehran and Washington were renewing dialogue boosted hopes of ending the Middle East war.
Iran on Monday said "intensive" exchanges were underway with Washington and offered to reopen the Strait of Hormuz under strict conditions, as efforts escalated to avert a return to conflict.
Earlier, the Axios news outlet reported that US Vice President JD Vance had sent a letter to Iranian national security chief Mohsen Rezaei about possible new talks.
That was the highest-level move from President Donald Trump's administration in months.
Again Capital's John Kilduff described investors as experiencing "a violent change in market sentiment," adding that "we went from really, I think, expecting a major offensive after tomorrow's US elections to a potential breakthrough," he told AFP.
"All these losses will be taken right back if this doesn't pan out," Kilduff said.
The steep drop in oil prices translated into weakness among petroleum stocks. But Wall Street shares otherwise began the day with promise, bouncing back after last Friday's rout precipitated by worries over the tech industry's massive artificial intelligence spending.
But tech shares came under pressure as the session progressed, with the tech-focused Nasdaq slumping 1.1 percent.
"This is still a market that is on edge," said Joseph Zidle, chief market strategist at Cresset Capital, who described unease about midterm elections as adding to worries about the AI boom.
"The two of them are actually related," Zidle said of midterms and AI, noting that opposition to data centers has animated many campaigns.
AI has been "on the ballot in so many places, both blue and red," Zidle said. "It seems like data centers are part of the kitchen table issues."
Pollsters expect Democrats to win back control of the House of Representatives, but view Trump's Republican party as potentially able to maintain a majority in the Senate.
The loss of total Republican dominance would push the president into unfamiliar and uncomfortable territory: a lame duck period beset with high inflation at home, the sputtering war against Iran and hostile Democratic investigations into his activities in Washington.
"Investors are bracing for a fresh round of turbulence ahead of US midterm election fireworks while they assess the extent that companies are burning through cash to keep the AI bonfires burning," said Susannah Streeter, chief investment strategist at Wealth Club.
Earnings this week will come from Apple, which reports after the close of trading on Monday, as well as Advanced Micro Devices and software titan Palantir will be closely watched this week. Shares in Apple fell 1.8 percent.

articles.title_orig: One dead after two helicopters collide near Mount Everest in Nepal
articles.title_zh: One dead after two helicopters collide near Mount Everest in Nepal
articles.content_orig:
Two helicopters have collided in Nepal’s Mount Everest region, killing at least one person and injuring two others.
The crash happened on Tuesday as both aircraft were attempting to land just below Mount Everest base camp. Mount Everest is the world’s tallest mountain above sea level.
Footage posted online shows more than a dozen people running to safety as the helicopters crashed into the ground following a collision.
Authorities have confirmed that a 47-year-old Indian national was killed. A New Zealand national and a Nepali pilot were injured. It is not clear how many people were on board the two helicopters.
The crash happened in Pheriche village, at an altitude of 4,200 metres (13,780 feet).
The Mount Everest region can be difficult to navigate because there are no roads. Helicopters are regularly used to evacuate trekkers and guides who have had to cut their journeys short because of sickness or exhaustion. Temperatures on the mountain always remain below freezing.
Last week, a fire broke out at a hotel along the route to Mount Everest base camp. Heavy snowfall hampered efforts to extinguish the blaze.
No deaths or injuries were reported in the fire.

The artificial intelligence infrastructure buildout will need more equity financing as lenders become increasingly exposed to the companies driving the buildout, Blackstone President Jon Gray said Tuesday.
Speaking at the Hong Kong Monetary Authority’s Global Financial Leaders’ Investment Summit, Gray said the scale of capital required for AI is creating concentration risks for debt investors, both across the sector and at individual companies.
Unlike shareholders, who can benefit from a company's growth, lenders have limited upside as their returns are largely confined to interest and principal repayments, he said.
Speaking at the same panel, Pimco CEO Emmanuel Roman warned investors that the scale of AI financing could prove to be "too much" for markets to absorb.
Roman said AI-related capital spending could reach around $10 trillion over the next five years, citing General Atlantic CEO Bill Ford's estimate. He added that about $550 billion in AI debt had been issued in various forms so far this year.
Even with a mix of equity and debt financing, the amount required would be “gigantic,” Roman said, comparing it with a global corporate bond market of roughly $20 trillion.
“At some point in time, it’s going to be too much,” he said.
Global data center demand will require about $8.5 trillion in capital spending over the next five years, Goldman Sachs wrote in a report Monday.
Gray said financing the buildout would require a combination of public markets, banks and private capital, with companies increasingly turning to structured transactions to limit the amount of debt they take on. Cash generated by hyperscalers would also fund part of the spending, he said.
“The creativity is needed because the scale of capital is enormous," Gray said.
Despite those financing challenges, Gray remained bullish on AI infrastructure, saying demand for computing power was “running well ahead of supply.”
Spending on AI models across Blackstone’s portfolio companies had risen 20-fold over the past year as businesses saw financial benefits from uses including coding, customer engagement and content creation, he said.
Meeting that demand remains difficult, however, as securing sites, permits, chips, power and capital becomes more challenging, according to Gray.

articles.title_orig: North Korea denies being behind $6.3bn Binance crypto hack
articles.title_zh: North Korea denies being behind $6.3bn Binance crypto hack
articles.content_orig:
North Korea has denied claims that it was behind the record $6.3bn (£4.7bn) hack of cryptocurrency exchange Binance , calling the allegations "absurd rhetoric".
Kim Yo Jong, a top Democratic People's Republic of Korea official and the sister of leader Kim Jong Un , said on Tuesday that the accusations are another "sinister attempt" by the US to damage Pyongyang's public image.
The US Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), the Secret Service and cyber analysts have said North Korea orchestrated the hack, which has been described as the largest in history.
This is the latest hack to be linked to North Korea, which has been accused of relying on cyber-crime to help finance its sanctioned economy.
Blockchain analysts and the FBI have said the attack was led by state-backed hacking group TraderTraitor.
The FBI has called on industry partners to help block transactions involving cryptocurrency accounts linked to the group.
"The US has made a trite provocation of linking it with the Democratic People's Republic of Korea again," Kim Yo-jong, the director of North Korea's General Affairs Department, said in a statement.
"It is a grave political provocation against the DPRK that the US misleads the international public opinion as if all the cyber crimes in different parts of the world are our deeds," she said.
But Pyongyang has been blamed for a number of major cyber attacks in recent years - accusations that it has denied.
The TraderTraitor unit, which is also known as the Lazarus Group, was blamed for a then-record $1.5bn hack of crypto exchange Bybit in 2025.
Pyongyang has systematically built its cyber operations, recruiting promising students from universities and sending them to hacker units overseen by North Korea's intelligence agency, research groups like the S Rajaratnam School of International Studies think tank have said.
The country has consistently denied such claims.
Kim Yo Jong said "it is the consistent policy stand of the DPRK government to resolutely oppose all sorts of malicious acts in cyberspace".
Binance did not respond to the BBC's queries about North Korea's alleged involvement in the hack.
Since the incident, the crypto giant has largely focused its public statements on the technical nature of the breach and its response to protect users.
The company's spokesperson said that a net $4.72bn has been withdrawn from the exchange since transactions resumed on Sunday.
The net outflow represents a "relatively limited portion"  of Binance's total assets, which stand at approximately $157bn, the spokesperson told the BBC on Tuesday.
That figure reflects the impact of the hack, subsequent withdrawals and market price changes.
"Withdrawal levels are stabilising to what we would consider normal and expected on-chain activity," she added.
The company said last week that initial checks indicated that an engineer's laptop had been compromised, enabling an attacker to make unauthorised withdrawals.
Trading in major cryptocurrencies on Binance has since resumed after the exchange worked with issuers to freeze assets impacted by the hack.
The company has repeatedly said it would cover all of the losses linked to the attack and that it has so far covered around 95% of the assets stolen in the breach.

articles.title_orig: Jeffrey Sachs On Economy, Ties With China & New World Order (Transcript)
articles.title_zh: Jeffrey Sachs On Economy, Ties With China & New World Order (Transcript)
articles.content_orig:
In this keynote at the Aristotle-Confucius Symposium in Varanasi, economist Jeffrey Sachs traces how Asia’s share of world production fell under European and American imperialism and why it is now returning to the center of the global economy. He talks about India-China ties, the rise of a multipolar world, family businesses and corporate responsibility, reviving the United Nations, and why the shared ethics of the world’s great traditions can help build a new world order of peace and cooperation. Read the full transcript of this lecture below:
JEFFREY SACHS: Good morning, friends. Doctor Adani, thank you for that brilliant address, but especially for all that you and your family and the foundation are doing for the world, which is very profound and very moving also to hear. And, Nirupam, thank you for the last thirty two years of collaboration and the continuing thirty two years of collaboration at least. I’m thrilled with all that we do together and most grateful. I want to thank the government of India, the Ministry of Culture.
I know the Secretary of Culture will be arriving shortly. His plane was diverted because of the fog this morning, but I think he’s landed and will arrive soon. I want to thank the partnership, of course, of the Adani Foundation and the Adani Group. And to pay my great respect to what the Adani Group is doing for sustainable development in India and globally because the scale of your work is remarkable as you just described, and it’s very, very inspiring. I’d like to thank TERI, which is a partner in organizing this symposium.
With TERI, we go back many decades of TERI’s leadership in sustainable development and in green energy and in climate safety. So it’s a tremendous joy to be working with TERI and joining together with TERI.
For me, it’s very moving to be here in Varanasi. Sonia and I first came here forty seven years ago. We fell in love with this magical place, which is one of the great, most holy places on the planet and one of the greatest centers of learning and knowledge and spirituality in the world, there’s probably not another place that combines such crucial world traditions as the place where we are.
So to be in Varanasi is absolutely extraordinary. We keep coming back, and we are inspired every time that we come together. And for me, it’s wonderful that so many of our colleagues and friends from this effort of ancient wisdom for modern challenges are together again here so that we can add, I think, significantly and profoundly to the depth of our work together and to help advance that work.
I’d like to spend a few minutes on the background of this symposium and why I think it’s so important. I have prepared remarks, which I will share with anyone that’s interested later, but I will not read them certainly right now.
I want to just share some basic thoughts with you. And I do need one slide, this one. So a lot of numbers, but the numbers… I’m an economist. I can’t help but look at some numbers.
But the numbers, I think, are absolutely key to understanding our world today. We are in a new territory in the world, not only because of AI or because of climate change or because of other technological disruptions that we face or being in the nuclear age, which is sad to say, perhaps the deepest reality of our world, which is the capacity to… Of humanity to end humanity in about seventy minutes as the current analyses show.
But we’re in a different world because history has moved in a very important and fundamental way, and that’s what these numbers help us to understand. So what you see here for several benchmark years starting in 1700 at the top row and then going to projections to 2100 to the end of the twenty first century in the bottom row, our estimates of the share of world production, this is a shorthand, but the share of the world product produced in different regions of the world.
And I’m showing you The United States, Europe, which in this case is the European Union plus Great Britain, China, and India. And I want you to see what has happened in history and what is happening today. Back in 1700, China and India each had about 20% of world production. Europe, about 24%. The United States didn’t exist yet.
It wouldn’t exist till the end of the example very to see be so of how that we’re world. The world economy. There’s obviously other places of not counted in this table to add up to a 100%.
As late as 1800, China was a third of world output more than Europe. India had already started to lose its share because India was already starting to be imperialized by Britain and by other European empires, which would be soon kicked out by Britain.
But India was being held back by the British Empire. China, not yet. It had not faced yet British imperialism that was to come starting in 1839. The United States now existed, and it was 1% of world output.
By 1900, the world had changed fundamentally because the nineteenth century was the century in which Europe temporarily dominated the world, and that was the world of European empire, not centuries long a century of domination of the nineteenth century.
And in that nineteenth century, of course, India fell entirely under British rule. China entered into what China calls the “century of humiliation,” which began with the… One of the most sordid wars of history, the war by Britain on China to force China to open up to actually British grown, India grown opium. It’s hard to imagine a more disgusting war than this, although I think the current Iran war ranks high as well, a war out of nothing.
But the Opium Wars started a century of disaster for China because two Opium Wars were followed by a massive civil war in China after those disruptions, known to us as the Taiping Rebellion, but really one of the largest civil wars in history.
And to cap that off at the end of the nineteenth century, Japan invaded China and began forty years of invasions of China so that there was catastrophe in both India and China.
Millions of people died in repeated famines in India completely unrelieved by the British Empire who stuck with a stiff upper lip to their laissez faire policy as people were dying and continued to export grains from famine stricken regions of this country.
So by 1900, Europe’s share of the world output was almost 40%. China and India together, and, of course, India being part of the British empire at that point, were now less than 20%.
So a decline to a mere 18% of world output for two countries that held more than 40% of the world population. 1950 was the nadir of Asia because this was a hundred fifty years of European and then American imperialism with American overseas imperialism starting in the eighteen nineties, first overthrowing the Kingdom of Hawaii and then taking the colony of The Philippines in the so called Spanish-American War.
Look at the situation in 1950. 56% of world output was in The United States and Europe, more than half. Whereas in China and India now combined on the independence of India and the independence of the People’s Republic Of China under 10% combined for two countries which still constituted more than 40% of world output.
That world of 1950 and the world that was created between 1800 and 1950 came to be seen as the norm of the world, that the West leads the world, the West designs the global realities, Asia is a small footnote under Western guidance, and this ideology was the prevailing ideology of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries. It’s the ideology that I grew up in myself and that I was trained in.
When I… When Sonia and I came to India in 1979, I was enthralled. This was a completely new world, an impoverished world, and I carried in my backpack a famous book of the time called “Asian Drama” by Gunnar Myrdal, which explained to me why Asia was poor and will always be poor.
This was the basic lesson of the “Asian Drama.” He won a Nobel Prize, certainly not for that. Most Nobel Prizes in economics are wrong anyway, but that one

articles.title_orig: UK to double wait for permanent residency, with exemptions for care workers
articles.title_zh: UK to double wait for permanent residency, with exemptions for care workers
articles.content_orig:
Al Jazeera investigation exposes paramilitary hitman linked to Turning Point UK
The United Kingdom has revised its immigration rules, doubling the time most foreign workers must wait to qualify for permanent residency to 10 years and making refugees who arrive on “small boats” wait as long as 30 years.
Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood, speaking in Parliament on Monday, said hundreds of thousands of care workers will be exempt from the hardline rules, offering a concession amid a political outcry within the governing Labour Party.
Permanent residency, known in the UK as indefinite leave to remain, carries the right to work, study, use the free National Health Service and claim welfare benefits. Until now, it has been granted after five years.
The new rules, set to take effect next year, tie eligibility for permanent residency to income.
People who earn more than 50,000 pounds a year ($67,000) will still be able to apply after five years, and those earning more than 125,000 pounds ($167,500) after three. Everyone else will be placed on the 10-year path. The median salary in the UK is about 39,000 pounds (roughly $52,000).
The rules will apply retroactively to workers already in the country.
“Settlement should not be automatic. It should be earned,” Mahmood, the home secretary, told Parliament, adding that the changes would restore fairness by linking the right to settle to what immigrants contribute.
“Those who contribute most will settle fastest,” she said. “Those who don’t play by the rules will be refused or wait longer.”
The UK government first proposed last year that lower-skilled workers wait 10 to 15 years for permanent residency.
But the plan drew fierce opposition from unions and parts of the Labour Party, particularly over its effect on care workers, who are often poorly paid and work in a sector that has long struggled to fill vacancies. Many of them arrived in the early 2020s, as the country was reeling from the COVID-19 pandemic, to fill gaps left by European workers who had departed after Brexit.
Under the revised plan, care workers will be able to settle after five years if they have met the conditions of their visas and earn at least 25,000 pounds ($33,500) a year.
Mahmood said the rules would offer a path for care workers “who worked hard and answered our call when we needed them”.
As for refugees, those who arrive through one of the government’s “new safe and legal routes” will be able to settle after five years, she said. For other refugees, the standard wait will become 20 years, reduced to 10 years for those who work or study. Anyone who arrived by an “illegal method”, such as by small boat, could wait up to 30 years for settlement, she said.
Under the new rules, applicants will also be disqualified if they have a criminal record, cannot speak English “to a high standard”, owe money to the government, or have not made at least three years of national insurance contributions.
Mahmood said the overhaul would mean that half a million people would settle later than they otherwise would have, saving the government billions of pounds in benefits.
In total, the government estimates that as many as 1.4 million people will receive settled status between 2026 and 2030.
The changes, announced after a 12-week public consultation that drew more than 200,000 responses, are part of a broader effort to tighten immigration rules after arrivals surged following Brexit.
They are a response to political pressure, including from Nigel Farage’s populist Reform UK party, which has surged in popularity in recent years with calls for stricter migration controls. Reform UK has sought to depict the arrivals of refugees on small boats across the English Channel as a crisis, and anti-immigration activists have staged protests, including outside facilities that house asylum seekers.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s government has said that increased law enforcement cooperation between the UK and France has helped reduce the number of people making the crossing so far this year by more than 40 percent compared with 2025.
