Oil prices tumbled more than seven percent on Monday, the eve of crucial midterm elections in the United States, as signals that Tehran and Washington were renewing dialogue boosted hopes of ending the Middle East war.
Iran on Monday said "intensive" exchanges were underway with Washington and offered to reopen the Strait of Hormuz under strict conditions, as efforts escalated to avert a return to conflict.
Earlier, the Axios news outlet reported that US Vice President JD Vance had sent a letter to Iranian national security chief Mohsen Rezaei about possible new talks.
That was the highest-level move from President Donald Trump's administration in months.
Again Capital's John Kilduff described investors as experiencing "a violent change in market sentiment," adding that "we went from really, I think, expecting a major offensive after tomorrow's US elections to a potential breakthrough," he told AFP.
"All these losses will be taken right back if this doesn't pan out," Kilduff said.
The steep drop in oil prices translated into weakness among petroleum stocks. But Wall Street shares otherwise began the day with promise, bouncing back after last Friday's rout precipitated by worries over the tech industry's massive artificial intelligence spending.
But tech shares came under pressure as the session progressed, with the tech-focused Nasdaq slumping 1.1 percent.
"This is still a market that is on edge," said Joseph Zidle, chief market strategist at Cresset Capital, who described unease about midterm elections as adding to worries about the AI boom.
"The two of them are actually related," Zidle said of midterms and AI, noting that opposition to data centers has animated many campaigns.
AI has been "on the ballot in so many places, both blue and red," Zidle said. "It seems like data centers are part of the kitchen table issues."
Pollsters expect Democrats to win back control of the House of Representatives, but view Trump's Republican party as potentially able to maintain a majority in the Senate.
The loss of total Republican dominance would push the president into unfamiliar and uncomfortable territory: a lame duck period beset with high inflation at home, the sputtering war against Iran and hostile Democratic investigations into his activities in Washington.
"Investors are bracing for a fresh round of turbulence ahead of US midterm election fireworks while they assess the extent that companies are burning through cash to keep the AI bonfires burning," said Susannah Streeter, chief investment strategist at Wealth Club.
Earnings this week will come from Apple, which reports after the close of trading on Monday, as well as Advanced Micro Devices and software titan Palantir will be closely watched this week. Shares in Apple fell 1.8 percent.

articles.title_orig: China expands swap and relending tools to steady the stock market
articles.title_zh: China expands swap and relending tools to steady the stock market
articles.content_orig:
China's central bank said it will run swap operations for brokers, fund managers and insurers as conditions warrant, pull in more participants, and trim the fees charged for those swaps. Alongside that, it will lower the interest rate on its relending program tied to share repurchases and stake building to 1% from 1.25%, make that facility a standing feature, and press banks to extend more credit through it.
Both tools debuted in October 2024. The relending channel supplies cheap central bank funding that banks use to make loans backing listed companies and major shareholders who are buying back stock or adding to stakes.
According to the securities regulator, the next swap tranche is expected to start shortly, and 31 approved brokerages and fund managers are together applying for quotas exceeding 100 billion yuan, or about $15 billion. The latest tally from the central bank shows swaps outstanding at 105 billion yuan, while roughly 440 billion yuan in loans tied to buybacks and stake-raising have been signed and over 280 billion yuan has already been paid out.
A meeting on the measures drew 23 securities firms and funds and 26 banks. Speakers included representatives from China International Capital Corp., Guotai Haitong Securities Co., Citic Securities Co., Industrial & Commercial Bank of China Ltd., China Construction Bank Corp. and China Citic Bank Corp.

The CSRC plans to broaden who can tap the relending program, including encouraging more companies that are major components of key indexes and more leading technology companies to participate. It also plans to ease buyback restrictions, allowing repurchases when shares fall under the IPO price, and mandating that firms holding surplus funds from capital raises carry out buybacks once market-support thresholds are triggered.
The regulator will study adjustments to margin financing - borrowing to buy stocks - to moderately raise financing capacity and help liquidity.
Beijing is leaning into a "slow bull" approach to entice household savings toward equities, but shaky market action has complicated that push, according to Gavekal Dragonomics. "The government wants to be seen as supportive, or investor confidence could decline even further," wrote Thomas Gatley and Xiaoxi Zhang, noting households remain cautious. The CSI 300 dropped 8.5% in October - its worst monthly fall in more than 10 years - and notched an unprecedented 12-week losing streak ending Friday.
In plain English: cheaper, permanent relending, more participants in the swap tool, looser buyback allowances and potential tweaks to margin financing all target one thing - steadier liquidity and incremental support for shares. Watch how quickly the coming swap tranche is allocated and how broad the relending coverage becomes, since the scale and speed will shape how much lift reaches Chinese equities.

articles.title_zh: U.S., Russia and Ukraine to resume peace talks in Abu Dhabi next week, Witkoff says
articles.content_orig:
Volodymyr Zelenskyy says attack in Komyshuvakha was ‘vile’ and shows Russia does not want to de-escalate
Russia on Monday bombed an aid distribution centre and neighbouring shelter in southern Ukraine , killing at least 26 ​people, Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy and the country’s emergency services said.
Emergency services said two members of a rescue crew and four police officers were among the dead in the village ⁠of Komyshuvakha, in south-eastern Zaporizhzhia region. Five people were being treated in hospital, including two rescue workers.
Zelenskyy, in his nightly video address, said Russian forces initially dropped bombs on a school in the village that was used as a shelter and for ⁠distributing humanitarian assistance.
There were no classes at the school, he said, as the village, lying south-east of the region’s main city, ​also called Zaporizhzhia, was too close to the frontline. ‌
“The Russians struck first ‌just as people were arriving – a few aerial bombs,” he said. “Then there was a second strike – more air bombs, this time on ‌the shelter. A vile terrorist strike.”
As night fell in Komyshuvakha, emergency responders used torches to search through the rubble of collapsed buildings, according to photos and video posted online by local officials. Regina Kharchenko, secretary of the Zaporizhzhia city council, said that 27 people were missing in the attack.
Efforts to rescue people Monday evening were hindered as Russian drones launched additional attacks in the area that had been bombed, according to Mykhailo Semikin, a military official in Zaporizhzhia.
Zelenskyy said the Russians could not have been unaware that residents remaining in Komyshuvakha gathered each week to pick up humanitarian packages from the site.
The attack, he said, had shown that Moscow was intent on killing people instead of building on the past week’s ceasefire in the embattled southern city of Oleshky , brokered by US first lady Melania Trump.
“Russians continue to demonstrate, time and again, their hatred of Ukraine and everything that exists here,” he said.
“If Russia genuinely ‌wanted de-escalation, there was an opportunity following the situation in Oleshky to continue taking humanitarian steps. We proposed this. But Russia continues to kill people.”
The ceasefire last week enabled an evacuation of the Russian-occupied Oleshky.
It was the longest pause in fighting between the neighbours in the war, now in its fifth year, which has killed hundreds of thousands of people and displaced millions.
The Kremlin said that no other similar missions were being planned “at the moment”.
US-led talks between Russia and Ukraine are set to resume next week, US special envoy Steve Witkoff said on Monday.
President Donald Trump has pushed for a settlement to the dragging war but there has been no breakthrough.
The talks – to be held 10 November and 11 in Abu Dhabi, Witkoff said – come as Kyiv and its European allies worry that Trump has increasingly sided with Moscow.
With Reuters, Associated Press and Agence France-Presse

articles.title_orig: Nvidia’s Huang Gave Blessing to Marvell-Lumentum Megadeal
articles.title_zh: Nvidia’s Huang Gave Blessing to Marvell-Lumentum Megadeal
articles.content_orig:
Marvell Technology 's deal for optical components maker Lumentum will create an "enormous" opportunity to address growing connectivity demands from the artificial intelligence infrastructure buildout, Lumentum CEO Michael Hurlston told CNBC on Monday.
"You need scale-up technology that needs semiconductors and optical working seamlessly together," Marvell CEO Matt Murphy told CNBC's "Squawk on the Street." "We are going to create a new category of company here."
Since the tie-up is a fixed-ratio deal with no cash, the value will depend on the price of Marvell shares. The company said the transaction has an implied enterprise value of $115 billion for Lumentum, in a release.
Marvell shares slumped 13% in trading Monday, while Lumentum's stock sank nearly 19%. But both stocks have been huge winners in the artificial intelligence boom, with Marvell more than doubling in the past year, prior to Monday's sell-off, and Lumentum quadrupling over that stretch.
Through the acquisition, Marvell said it can combine electrical and optical technologies to meet accelerating and shifting AI connectivity demands across regions and systems. Companies are increasingly relying on optical connections to piece together chips used to run and train large language models.
"We're actually going to create solutions around those that are highly sticky, and the reason that they're sold out is because the demand is exploding, and we don't see that changing anytime soon," Murphy said.
Lumentum shareholders will receive 4.5 Marvell shares for each Lumentum share under the agreement. The deal is expected to close during the first half of 2028.
Marvell's takeover marks one of the most significant bets on AI in 2026 and comes despite recent concerns over the long-term sustainability of infrastructure spending.
This isn't the company's first bet on AI growth. This year, the company closed a multibillion-dollar deal for Celestial AI, a startup focused on optical interconnectivity technology.
Marvell 's Murphy also shot down concerns about Nvidia's circular dealmaking, given the leading AI chipmaker's recent multibillion-dollar investments in both companies.
In a bid to further support the data center infrastructure that houses its AI chips, Nvidia has positioned itself as a central cog in a network of related companies, investing in several technology companies that purchase its chips or neoclouds that rent out computing capacity. That's sparked criticism that companies like Nvidia are virtually funding themselves by taking stakes in customers.
"This is a double down on supporting Nvidia, who is the ecosystem leader in this area," Murphy told CNBC. "We're very committed to that partnership, and I think having two of the key suppliers come together, that support that ecosystem, is going to be a big benefit for them."
Marvell has seen its market value more than triple over the last three years, buoyed by unrelenting AI enthusiasm. Lumentum's stock has more than doubled in 2026 alone.
CORRECTION: This story has been updated to reflect that Lumentum CEO Michael Hurlston described the deal as an 'enormous' opportunity. A previous version of this story incorrectly cited the Marvell CEO.

articles.title_orig: Trump to remove Rwanda and South Africa from US trade deal
articles.title_zh: Trump to remove Rwanda and South Africa from US trade deal
articles.content_orig:
Last year, Trump accused South Africa of white genocide in a meeting with President Cyril Ramaphosa at the White House
US President Donald Trump has notified Congress of his intention to remove South Africa and Rwanda from a preferential trade programme, from 1 January 2027.
The African Growth and Opportunity Act (Agoa) allows eligible African countries to export thousands of products to the US duty-free.
US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said in a statement that an annual review had found that both countries were engaging in practices inconsistent with the programme's eligibility requirements.
He added that the Trump administration had additionally notified the two countries of the decision.
The Trump administration cited barriers to US trade and investment, as well as concerns over national security and foreign policy interests in the region.
For South Africa, the US pointed to corruption.
"The Trump administration is working to ensure our African partners take the necessary steps to meet the eligibility criteria," Greer said.
South Africa's Trade Minister Parks Tau described the decision as "unfortunate", saying Washington was raising new issues that had not featured in trade negotiations between the two countries, which began in 2025.
"We will continue to accelerate the diversification of South Africa's export markets to protect jobs," Tau said.
US Ambassador to South Africa Leo Brent Bozell III said it was regrettable that South African policies led to its termination from Agoa.
"This was a predictable and preventable outcome resulting from the rejection by South Africa's government of real concerns raised by the US," he wrote on X.
The announcement comes amid strained relations between Washington and both countries, with the proposed termination threatening their access to preferential trade arrangements with the US.
Last year, Trump accused South Africa of persecuting its white minority and launched a programme for white Afrikaners to get asylum in the US.
Trump also repeated widely discredited claims of a genocide of South Africa's white population.
South African white genocide does not exist, new ambassador to US tells BBC
Is there a genocide of white South Africans as Trump claims?
In Rwanda's case, Washington also raised concerns about human rights, political pluralism, the rule of law and workers' rights.
The move comes barely a week after Rwanda's defence ministry was hit with sanctions by US Treasury for its alleged role in the armed rebellion in eastern DR Congo .
The US Treasury said Rwanda's defence ministry directed thousands of troops to fight alongside M23 rebels in eastern DR Congo, providing weapons, equipment, logistics and training.
Rwanda has denied backing the M23 despite overwhelming evidence.

articles.title_orig: How To Quit Spotify And Improve Your Life In The Process
articles.title_zh: How To Quit Spotify And Improve Your Life In The Process
articles.content_orig:
It's a lot easier than you're probably thinking
Having already been in the news over the past few years for not paying artists, laying off its own workforce and supporting the genocide in Palestine , Spotify was once again in the news this week for shitty reasons, specifically that the company is about to roll out a ghoulish AI-powered remix/cover feature .
The best time and reason to ditch Spotify was when any of that other stuff came to light. The second-best time is today , so in the spirit of telling this company to get in the bin here's a guide to getting off Spotify and, more importantly, getting your music somewhere else.
1) Choose which competitor you'd like to use instead. If you want to stop streaming altogether, buying albums directly off Bandcamp is a great way to support an artist directly. If you can't shake your dependency on streaming catalogues, there are plenty of alternatives like Tidal, Apple Music and Qobuz. I would not recommend Amazon or YouTube Music for both obvious (both companies suck) and technical reasons (they're bad apps, and YT Music has terrible sound quality).
2) If your new service supports it directly (Apple Music on iOS does, for example), you can sometimes just transfer your Spotify library straight over. If it doesn't, you can use a service like Free Your Music or TuneMyMusic , which might cost you a few bucks but in the grand scheme of things is worth the investment. Those tools will do their best (and by experience they're very good) at moving your whole library, playlists and all, off Spotify and over to your new platform of choice. If you also listened to podcasts within Spotify, most rivals will also offer podcasts within their music app, but if they don't--Android users can't use Apple Podcasts, for example--Pocket Casts is a totally workable solution.
3) Once your library has transferred, delete your Spotify account, then block their email addresses, because after a few weeks they'll start sending you pathetic offers like this:
4) That's it. What, were you expecting some long, drawn-out, 2000-word guide? It's extremely easy to get off Spotify while keeping your library intact, and you don't owe that company shit. What are you waiting for.
Luke Plunkett is a co-founder of the website Aftermath.

articles.title_orig: US to mediate new round of negotiations to end Russia-Ukraine war
articles.title_zh: US to mediate new round of negotiations to end Russia-Ukraine war
articles.content_orig:
De-escalation, post-war security and humanitarian efforts on the agenda of trilateral talks. What we know on day 1,714
The US will bring together ⁠delegations from Ukraine and Russia in Abu Dhabi next week for talks on ending Moscow’s ⁠war against Ukraine , US envoy Steve Witkoff has said. In ​a social media post, ‌Witkoff said the discussions will cover “post-war security agreements, de-escalation, humanitarian measures, and ending ‌the war”. Witkoff and Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner are expected to represent the US at the talks, Reuters quoted a senior US official as saying. Russian president Vladimir Putin agreed to a new round of trilateral talks after meeting Witkoff in St Petersburg ‌two weeks ago.
Witkoff also said in his post that US negotiators would meet this week in Brussels with representatives from the UK, France, Germany, the EU and Nato to discuss “security guarantees for Ukraine, Europe’s postwar security architecture and economic opportunities to support Ukraine’s reconstruction”. Ukraine ​and Russia ​remain far apart on the terms of any possible peace deal. The last US-mediated trilateral peace talks took place in February before ⁠the US and Israel launched a war against Iran.
Russia launched a huge overnight ⁠strike ⁠on Ukrainian ​energy facilities in ⁠the Vinnytsia, Dnipropetrovsk and Kharkiv ⁠regions, the Interfax ​news agency ‌said ‌on Tuesday, ‌citing the Russian defence ministry. Moscow’s ‌forces also hit port infrastructure ​in the Odesa region and ⁠vessels used ​for military purposes, it said. ⁠In ⁠the ​Russian city of ⁠Yaroslavl, ​an oil refinery was damaged in ⁠a ​Ukrainian ‌drone ‌attack, local governor ‌Mikhail Evrayev said. Two ‌employees were injured and emergency ​services were working to ⁠put out ​a fire ​at the site, ‌he ​added. The reports could not immediately be verified.
On Monday, Russian forces bombed a school used as an aid distribution point in ⁠a village in Ukraine’s south-eastern ⁠Zaporizhzhia region, killing 26 ​people , Volodymyr Zelenskyy and the country’s emergency services said. ‌“The Russians struck first ‌just as people were arriving – a few aerial bombs,” the Ukrainian president said. “Then there was a second strike – more air bombs, this time on ‌the shelter. A vile terrorist strike.”
About 2,800 troops from 10 European countries will this month stage in Poland the first exercise of a new multinational force in support of Ukraine , London and Paris said on Tuesday. Led by France and the UK, the “Multinational Force – Ukraine” (MNF-U) has no offensive mission and is only to be deployed once a ceasefire is agreed to end the war triggered by Russia’s 2022 invasion. “The exercise will allow the testing of the speed and efficiency at which several nations can deploy forces on land, sea and air to support Ukraine once hostilities have finished,” the joint statement released by the French defence ministry said. “This isn’t a hypothetical plan, it’s a real force, ready to help Ukraine once the fighting stops,” the UK defence minister, Wes Streeting, was quoted as saying in the UK statement. The exercise is scheduled to run from 9-22 November in south-east Poland, not far from the Ukrainian border.
Unknown hackers targeted Ukraine’s nationwide emergency alert mobile app , sending residents in Kyiv a warning that they were at risk of an imminent nuclear strike. It also wrongly warned of a chemical threat to the Ukrainian capital and street-to-street fighting, Luke Harding reports . “I was briefly terrified,” one woman said.
Ukraine has accused Russia of taking advantage of the US-backed humanitarian ceasefire last week in the southern Kherson region to strengthen ⁠its military position there. Nearly 800 people ⁠ were evacuated from the ​Russian-occupied Ukrainian town of Oleshky, according to US first lady Melania Trump, who the White House says brokered the truce. Both sides have praised the six-day pause in fighting around the town as a success. But on Monday Kyiv’s general staff said Russian forces had also used the truce to rotate troops, boost defences and improve battlefield logistics. Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry ‌Peskov said he did not have specific information on any movements, but that adjusting positions during a ceasefire was “standard practice” and it ‌was safe to assume Ukraine had done the same.

Iran said Monday it had a two-day plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and resume nuclear talks with the United States, shortening a process originally expected to take seven days.
The U.N. migration agency said more than 300,000 people in Yemen had fled renewed fighting. China , meanwhile, is sending a special envoy to Iran, Saudi Arabia and Oman .
Here is the latest news from the Middle East on Monday. Read our full coverage here.
Iran's 2-day plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, resume nuclear talks
Iran said it had a two-day plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and resume nuclear talks with the U.S. if Washington meets its demands.
The announcement came as the region braces for possible renewed fighting, even as Iran’s top diplomat said Sunday that he hoped the U.S. would choose “diplomacy over other paths.”
Iran previously said the plan could be implemented within a week if the U.S. met seven conditions, including lifting its blockade of Iranian ports. Iran now says ships passing through the reopened strait would have to follow a route agreed upon by Iran and Oman and travel under Iranian supervision. Separately, Iranian officials have said the U.S. must lift sanctions on Iranian oil sales and agree to a ceasefire that would include Lebanon.
Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmail Baghaei said the plan remained the basis for negotiations with Washington through mediators, despite the shorter implementation timeline. “This once again demonstrates Iran’s good-faith approach,” he added.
Baghaei gave no indication that Tehran had changed its demands or that Washington had accepted its proposal.
President Donald Trump has alternated between pursuing diplomacy and threatening heavy bombing of Iran in his public comments.
More than 300,000 Yemenis have fled fighting, UN says
The U.N. migration agency said the people are struggling to find shelter and life essentials, as aid groups face limited access to those in need.
They have fled as renewed fighting between Iran-backed Houthi rebels and the Saudi-backed government forces broke a four-year truce, exacerbating an already dire humanitarian situation in one of the Middle East's poorest countries.
Taiz province, in southwestern Yemen, continues to take in displaced families, but many are fleeing south to Aden, which has now received more than 56,000 people, according to the latest figures by the International Organization for Migration.
“After years of conflict, families in Yemen are being forced to flee yet again, often with little more than the clothes on their backs,” Abdusattor Esoev, head of the IOM's mission in Yemen, said Sunday.
“They urgently need shelter, food, clean water and health care. Without more funding, thousands of families could be left without the help they urgently need,” he added.
China to send special envoy to Iran and the Gulf
China said Monday it plans to send a special envoy to Iran, Oman and Saudi Arabia in early to mid-November. Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning told reporters the envoy would focus on easing tensions and promoting regional stability.
The Gulf region “should not become an arena for great-power rivalry and geopolitical conflict,” Chinese President Xi Jinping told Oman’s Sultan Haitham bin Tariq Al Said on Monday, according to a readout of their meeting.
The move comes as China seeks to expand its influence in the rapidly changing region, which it depends on for a large share of its oil.
Two Israeli airstrikes killed two men in southern Gaza early Monday, according to Nasser Hospital, where their bodies were taken. One strike killed a man in his home; the other killed a man in a tent.
The Israeli military did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Major fighting between Israel and Hamas largely halted under the October 2025 ceasefire. Israel continues to launch near-daily strikes on Gaza that it says target militants, though the strikes regularly kill or injure women and children. Israel says Hamas uses civilians as human shields.
About 1,580 Palestinians have been killed since the ceasefire began, bringing the overall death toll to more than 74,500, according to Gaza’s Health Ministry. The ministry, part of the Hamas-run government, does not distinguish between civilians and militants.

articles.title_orig: Long March leaves its footprints in British libraries
articles.title_zh: Long March leaves its footprints in British libraries
articles.content_orig:
Xinhua |
          Updated: 2026-11-03 08:54
LONDON — In a reading room at the British Library, a blue stamp dated Jan 27, 1937, appears inside a book written by a British missionary who witnessed part of China's Long March.
Nearly 90 years later, the book offers a glimpse into how the extraordinary journey of the Chinese Red Army reached readers thousands of miles away.
As this year marks the 90th anniversary of the victory of the Long March, a remarkable revolutionary feat achieved under the leadership of the Communist Party of China, libraries and archives across Britain, along with the recollections of a writer who retraced the historic route, offer fresh perspectives on a journey that helped shape modern China.
At London's Marx Memorial Library, founded in 1933, two early publications shed light on how the Chinese Red Army was portrayed to British readers.
One is Edgar Snow's Red Star Over China, published in Britain in 1937. Its orange-red cover bears the words "LEFT BOOK CLUB EDITION" and "NOT FOR SALE TO THE PUBLIC".
Snow's account introduced Western readers to the CPC, its leaders and the extraordinary hardships endured by Red Army soldiers during the Long March.
Another is Agnes Smedley's China's Red Army Marches, published in London in 1936. Focusing on the Red Army's activities before its historic journey, the book describes villagers making shoes for soldiers and farmers delivering rice to support them.
One passage even reproduces a revolutionary song, complete with musical notation, preserving the voices of Chinese soldiers in a book published thousands of miles away.
The British Library also holds a 1937 edition of Snow's book bearing a stamp from the former India Office Library dated Oct 30, 1937.
Contemporary British newspapers also reflected growing interest in the Red Army. On Oct 19, 1937, the Edinburgh Evening News published a review of Snow's book, devoting a section specifically to the Long March.
Together, these publications offered British readers accounts of the soldiers' experiences, their daily lives and the circumstances surrounding their remarkable journey, bringing distant events in China into view for the British public.
At the University of East Anglia in Norwich, eastern England, three archival boxes preserve the story of Alfred Bosshardt, a British missionary who accompanied the Red Army through parts of southwestern China.
Bosshardt's experiences were later recounted in The Restraining Hand, published in Britain in 1936, making him one of the earliest Western eyewitnesses to record aspects of the Long March.
The university's collection contains hundreds of items, including correspondence, photographs, newspaper cuttings and audiovisual recordings. Many were collected by British journalist and writer Anthony Grey, who helped bring Bosshardt's story to a wider audience.
Despite their different beliefs, Bosshardt developed considerable respect for the Red Army soldiers, particularly for their discipline and determination.
He recalled that soldiers were instructed to respect villagers, pay for food and compensate residents for damaged property. During breaks from their arduous journey, young soldiers sang songs, wrestled and shared moments of laughter.
Bosshardt also admired Red Army commander Xiao Ke, with whom he later renewed contact. Their friendship continued for decades, forming a remarkable personal link between Britain and China.
Nearly seven decades after the Long March, British-based Chinese writer Sun Shuyun spent 14 months retracing the odyssey. Traveling through remote villages, she interviewed surviving Red Army veterans and their families in an effort to understand the people behind the historical narrative.
For Sun, who studied history at the University of Oxford, the journey became one of the most unforgettable experiences of her life.
In East China's Jiangxi province, she met an elderly woman who had persuaded her newlywed husband to join the Red Army. He never returned. Nearly 70 years later, she was still waiting for him.
In Northwest China's Gansu province, Sun interviewed a former female Red Army soldier whose life had been marked by poverty, captivity and hardship.
The elderly woman welcomed Sun into her home, wrapped her in thick blankets and prepared a meal unusually rich in salt. Her adopted daughter explained that salt had been extremely scarce during the Long March, leaving the woman with a lifelong habit of cherishing it.
Recalling these encounters at her London home, Sun was moved to tears.
She said the Long March demonstrated the CPC's organizational strength and leadership and laid an important foundation for the eventual victory of the Chinese revolution.
"The Long March is one of the most important events in modern Chinese history," she said, adding that its legacy continues to resonate with China's development today.
Sun stressed that the choices and sacrifices of ordinary people, whose experiences could sometimes be overlooked in historical narratives, deserve to be remembered and passed down to future generations.
From the hardships of revolutionary struggle to the achievements of modernization, the Chinese people have continued to undertake new journeys requiring courage and perseverance, she said.
The great spirit of the Long March "will always deserve to be remembered", Sun added.

articles.title_orig: PM plans debt re-set for Commonwealth nations as slavery apology talks begin
articles.title_zh: PM plans debt re-set for Commonwealth nations as slavery apology talks begin
articles.content_orig:
The prime minister will join the King at the formal opening of the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting in Antigua later - and begin talks with fellow leaders about the UK issuing a formal apology for the slave trade in the next year.
As part of the discussions, Downing Street said Andy Burnham would set out his plans for what it is calling a "debt reset" to support Commonwealth countries having to deal with the growing costs of paying interest on their debts.
The issue of reparations, compensation to those who were the victims of slavery, has dominated debate in the build up to this summit, in which representatives from 56 Commonwealth countries are meeting.
"Britain is bringing a new approach to this meeting," the prime minister said, in a tacit acknowledgement that the last Commonwealth gathering, on the Pacific island of Samoa two years ago, did not go well from a UK perspective.
The previous Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer had said prior to the meeting that reparations were not on the agenda , but other leaders insisted they should be.
This time, the new prime minister has sought to get ahead of the debate, and appeared to directly address the anger of some Commonwealth leaders after the last summit.
"For years, those members of the Commonwealth affected by the slave trade have asked for an honest conversation about the legacies of slavery . By sticking our heads in the sand, we have damaged the ability of the Commonwealth to function," Burnham argued in an article in the Guardian.
Burnham alongside the Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband and the former Prime Minister Gordon Brown, are beginning conversations which, they hope, will help detoxify the debate about reparations.
They do so while insisting the UK will not pay them, but is likely to formally apologise for the slave trade for the first time next year, when the UK holds the rotating presidency of the G20 group of countries.
"A formal apology," Miliband said in a social media video , is something "the British government are open to".
He said this would be a "significant step" but added that "we don't believe financial reparations are the right or feasible answer to transatlantic slavery. We don't think the right response is to ask British taxpayers today to make financial payments for these historic acts."
The Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has urged the prime minister not to issue an apology for slavery, saying it would give countries a reason to ask the UK for reparations.
She said: "I don't think we should be giving any money to compensate people for the slave trade, and I don't think that Andy Burnham needs to be apologising because it is a lever to wedge open the door to ask for cash."
But British officials are hopeful, even confident, that the prime minister and foreign secretary's approach will create space in the next two days for a wider conversation with fellow Commonwealth countries.
No 10 said the UK would lead two new task forces - one focused on critical mineral assets and vulnerabilities in supply chains across the group and the other aimed at boosting trade and investment more widely.
Both will be set up by the end of the year and report back at the next leaders' summit, officials said.
British diplomats view the Commonwealth as a useful forum for conversations with developing countries, and, crucially, one that does not involve China, America or Russia.

articles.title_orig: Iran says contacts over ending war continue after talks finish with no breakthrough
articles.title_zh: Iran says contacts over ending war continue after talks finish with no breakthrough
articles.content_orig:
Brent crude drops by more than 6% to $105.55 a barrel, the lowest level in more than two weeks
The oil price has fallen to its lowest level in more two weeks amid new hopes of a breakthrough to end the Iran war.
Brent crude, the international benchmark, dropped by more than 6.5% to as low as $105.55 a barrel on Monday, the lowest since 16 October, sending shares in airline companies higher and pushing down government borrowing costs.
Oil prices fell after Tehran revealed that contacts between Iran and the US to end their eight-month war were continuing.
“Consultations through mediators are very ⁠intensive. We have presented our conditions and ⁠proposals and everything depends on the political ​rationality of Washington,” the Iranian foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, said, according to the state media outlet IRNA.
Over the weekend, Qatari officials tried to negotiate the release of more than $6bn (£4.5bn) in Iranian assets , so that Tehran might allow the strait of Hormuz to reopen.
On Monday, US vice-president JD Vance reported that there had been “a number of good conversations with the Iranians” and that he was feeling good about the prospects of a “negotiated settlement”.
Vance sent a letter to Iran’s security chief, Mohsen Rezaei, last week but the White House has offered few details about the contents of that correspondence.
Donald Trump had earlier taken a belligerent tone, telling voters in Iowa on Sunday that Iran would receive “the hammer” unless there was progress.
“The only reason why I’m not finished with Iran is I want to be nice. I want to try and save all those lives if I can ... But at some point we’re going to have to give them the hammer,” he said during a campaign rally in the run-up to the US midterm elections.
But investors were cheered by reports on Monday that Iran’s supreme leader, Mojtaba Khamenei, had granted “powers” to his government in its talks with the US seeking to end the Middle East war.
after newsletter promotion
Chris Beauchamp, the chief market analyst at the investing and trading platform IG, said: “The news is manna from heaven for stock markets, which have felt increasingly pressured by oil’s rise, but of course there is still a risk that Trump will try one last throw of the iron dice after the midterms.”
The drop in the oil price sparked hopes of a break in the inflationary pressures gripping the global economy. Government borrowing costs dropped, with the yield – or interest rate – on 10-year UK bonds down 10 basis points, or 0.1 of a percentage point, to the lowest since 22 September.
Shares in British Airways’ parent company, IAG, rose by 4.2% in London, while United Airlines jumped 7% in New York.

articles.title_orig: Two Chinese Nationals Receive Less Than Three Years Prison Time for Spying on US Navy
articles.title_zh: Two Chinese Nationals Receive Less Than Three Years Prison Time for Spying on US Navy
articles.content_orig:
The pair was accused of gathering information about U.S. military personnel and facilitating secret cash payments.
Two Chinese nationals have been sentenced to 30 months in prison for acting as illegal agents of the People’s Republic of China after conducting surveillance operations targeting U.S. Navy personnel and military facilities.
Their charges are conspiring to act as agents of the PRC government and acting as agents of a foreign government without prior notification to the Attorney General.
One of the convicted criminals, Liren “Ryan” Lai, was arrested in Houston last year.
According to court documents, Lai and co-defendant Yuance Chen of Oregon began acting as agents under a Chinese intelligence officer with PRC’s Ministry of State Security in 2021.
Authorities alleged that the pair photographed U.S. military personnel and facilities, Navy recruiting offices, and naval installations in Washington and California.
They also reportedly attempted to recruit other potential MSS members from the U.S. military.
“Chen and Lai operated as illegal agents for the Chinese government on U.S. soil, carrying out clandestine intelligence work that included making covert payments, collecting sensitive military information, and attempting to recruit American service members,” said Assistant Director Roman Rozhavsky of the FBI’s Counterintelligence and Espionage Division.
Their activities included secret “dead drop” cash payments in exchange for intelligence related to the national security of the U.S.
A dead drop of $10,000 was reportedly sent to Chen. The MSS also directed Lai to travel to Phoenix in 2025 to facilitate a cash payment of $20,000.
An unsealed federal affidavit cited an incident that involved Chen surveilling the Naval Special Warfare Command in San Diego, which oversees Navy SEALs.
The pair were arrested on June 27, 2025, in a coordinated FBI counterintelligence and law enforcement operation.
A federal grand jury in the Northern District of California returned an indictment charging both defendants with conspiracy to act as agents of a foreign government without prior notification to the attorney general and acting as agents of a foreign government without prior notification.
Both pleaded guilty and received sentences of 30 months in prison and three years of supervised release.
“Lai’s and Chen’s activities, undertaken at the direction of the PRC, were extensive and brazen. The National Security Division is committed to holding accountable anyone who aids or abets such espionage efforts,” said Assistant Attorney General for National Security John A. Eisenberg.
Rozhavsky noted that while “The Chinese government’s efforts to infiltrate our armed forces demonstrate just how far it will go to threaten U.S. national security,” the country has “underestimated the FBI’s commitment to thwarting its illegal activity and holding its agents accountable.”
“Let this sentencing serve as a clear warning: If you attempt to jeopardize the safety and security of our service members, our citizens, or our nation, justice will find you,” added Rozhavsky.

Duo is constrained as of today. The ramp is going well, and we're working hard to get it to as many customers as quickly as possible, but at this point, we're not able to predict when supply and demand will be in balance.

articles.title_orig: Review: Stellar Blade: Complete Edition (Switch 2) - Perfectly Playable, Despite Drawbacks
articles.title_zh: Review: Stellar Blade: Complete Edition (Switch 2) - Perfectly Playable, Despite Drawbacks
articles.content_orig:
Though the genre has evolved and deepened over time, gacha games have historically not been praised for their depth and complexity, often being criticised for being thinly veiled gambling machines. People were understandably incredulous, then, when Shift Up — the studio behind Goddess of Victory: Nikke — announced in 2019 that it would pursue a AAA passion project called Stellar Blade . Even more were then shocked a few years later when this wildly different, ambitious project turned out to be a pretty solidly made action game.
Stellar Blade has now been ported to Switch 2 (along with some cheeky new cosmetic Bayonetta DLC), bringing this titillating and gripping action experience to the Nintendo audience. It hasn’t made the transition to more modest hardware completely unscathed, but this is nonetheless a solidly enjoyable and thrilling adventure that deserves a spot in your library.
The narrative is set in the distant, post-apocalypse future, when our planet has been overrun by monstrous creatures called Naytibas. Some humans escaped after losing the war and established a space-based orbital colony called…the Colony…from which occasional squadrons of elite super-soldiers are deployed to attempt to regain a foothold on Earth.
Protagonist Eve is a member of one of these squads and the prologue opens with her landing mission, a violent meatgrinder reminiscent of the Omaha Beach scene in Saving Private Ryan in which she’s seemingly the sole warrior who survives. Aided by a mysterious man who saved her, Eve sets out to track down the Alpha Naytiba and hopefully notch a win for the humans.
It’s a decently entertaining story, but one which feels a little surface-level in many ways. Characters — Eve included — lack depth and converse in a stilted way that sounds as if they’re quoting lines at each other, and some of the later plot twists are the sort of thing that you can see coming a mile away. Yet there’s just enough lore here to keep you interested in the setting and Eve’s ongoing journey and occasional moments of levity help to keep things from feeling too dour.
Any disappointment with the storytelling is quickly forgotten by the thrill of combat, which feels like a cross between a Soulslike and a character action game as Eve deftly combos enemies with her athletic acrobatics and expert sword strikes.
Enemies hit hard and fast and can easily stunlock you, meaning that even a single average foe can take quite a large chunk out of your health bar if you're not paying careful attention and multiple foes at once can rapidly overwhelm Eve due to limited mobility and crowd control options.
Along with the usual combos you can string together with light and heavy attacks, Eve also has a variety of limited-use Beta Skills she can use to turn the tide in her favour. You build up Beta Energy from attacks and perfectly timed blocks or parries, and this energy can then be burned mid-combo to either bolster an attack or use a flashy guard-breaking attack that can put the enemy on the back foot. This system adds a nice bit of room for player skill expression, as you can find some creative ways to weave together combos and Beta Skills to positively melt foes.
Though even common enemies can put you to the test in certain configurations, this combat system really sings when you get to one of the many cinematic boss fights against powerful, grotesque monsters. These act as occasional hard skill checks that will forcibly teach you deeper knowledge of combat mechanics as you carefully study their movesets for brief gaps and learn (often across multiple failed attempts) how to best exploit those gaps with your available tools.
Eve thus feels both all-powerful and vulnerable at the same time, which lends combat encounters a thrilling and electric feel as you oscillate between slicing enemies to ribbons with practised cinematic flair and getting absolutely folded when you mis-time a dodge. Practice makes perfect, and there's lots of satisfaction that comes from progressing across the hours and going up against increasingly more complicated and dangerous foes with sharpened reflexes and skill.
Yet progress happens in more ways than just raw skill development - there are also some light RPG elements that allow you to slowly shape Eve's build over time. Not only can you use skill points to unlock and power up new combat abilities and Beta Skills, but you can also improve stats like max health and attack through finding collectibles in the environment.
Gear can also be found and crafted to give Eve certain passive buffs, allowing you to get more value out of the playstyle you generally choose. These RPG mechanics help to soften some of the harder edges of the often unforgiving combat system, giving you meaningful ways to progress over time even if you struggle greatly with losing battles to enemies.
World and level design initially follows traditional Soulslike tropes, consisting of lots of claustrophobic halls and labyrinthine paths that often loop back on each other with unlocked doors and ladders that lead back to the nearest checkpoint. While the critical path is usually obvious and easy to follow, there are often a handful of side areas to explore along the way rife with more platforming gauntlets, challenging enemy placements and extra upgrades and goodies. This design does a great job of rewarding exploration while keeping you moving forward.
Then, roughly six or so hours in, things change up with the sudden introduction of a medium-sized open-world area, filled with quests, collectibles, and points of interest to scour. Travelling between this area and a nearby hub has both gameplay and narrative benefits, as you complete quests and bounties to progress various side storylines for NPCs living there and find increasingly better gear and unlockables as quest and exploration rewards.
It admittedly seems at first like a weird left turn after the opening hours set very different expectations, but ultimately feels like a worthy addition to the gameplay loop. And even after its introduction, there are plenty of returns to the more focused and level-based Soulslike design, which balances out the free but occasionally meandering levels and quests that can come with the open world.
Graphics look decent, but not exceptional, due in part to both the overall art direction and the Switch 2’s relatively modest hardware. Some of the vistas of the ruined Earth can be quite nice to look at from afar, but there’s a lot of muted colours utilised as you trawl through tunnels, sewers, deserts, and destroyed office buildings. Environments thus tend to blend together and often lack visually interesting landmarks or set pieces, which can make the sections more focused on exploration a little more dull.
Meanwhile, the game outputs at 720p handheld and 1080p docked, which can lead to visuals that look even more muddy due to the upscaling artifacting and relatively low internal resolutions.
Regarding performance, everything technically runs at 60fps, but there's a pretty massive caveat with that claim: this frame rate is only accomplished through frame generation. Practically speaking, this means that there's a significant amount of input lag despite the visuals themselves appearing to animate smoothly. For a game this focused on quick reaction times and granular movement, that input lag can be a death knell and does noticeably reduce the playability of this port.
However, there is an option in the settings to turn this off and reduce the game to what appears to be closer to 40fps, which feels like a much more acceptable compromise. Controls are quite a bit more responsive here, while the frame rate is noticeably smoother than 30fps. There are some drops that can still happen when panning the camera around in larger areas, but it doesn’t overly affect the playability of combat encounters and this becomes less of an issue in the many smaller environments.
All this is to say, Stellar Blade is a game

articles.content_orig:
Country music star Parker McCollum tells OutKick OutDoors how he harvested the buck of a lifetime during Oklahoma's archery season, including the moment a can of ZYN nearly spooked the deer.
Part of getting out in nature is witnessing some nature. A group of people in Redwood National Park had a front row seat to some nature when a couple of bucks smashing antlers came tumbling down the side of a hill.
The hikers were "just exploring the Redwood forest" when the nature arrived. After sliding across the boardwalk, the two deer resumed their battle just a few feet away from the group, who, let's be honest, were way too close for comfort.
A dense sequoia forest with a boardwalk beneath the trees. (Getty Images/iStockphoto)
The deer tossed each other around the woods a little, you know classic rutting season behavior , before launching each other over the side of another small hill. The commentary on this now-viral battle is amazing.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE FROM OUTKICK OUTDOORS
The only thing better than the up-close and personal battle, and the play-by-play that accompanied it, is the comment section on the Instagram post .
Here we are being sucked back in by technology while trying to enjoy nature. It just goes to show you that not all technology is bad.
Bridge 1 on the Main Trail in Muir Woods National Monument on Mount Tamalpais in Marin County, Calif. The parkland is part of the Golden Gate National Recreation Area. (Getty Images/iStockphoto)
A place where you can weigh in with thoughts like "Shoulda started taking bets on the trail. Missed opportunity" still has some value.
COYOTES CHOOSE THE FRONT OF A COUPLE'S SOUTHERN CALIFORNIA CABIN FOR AN EARLY MORNING SCRAP
Where else would we go for the delicate balance of slightly useful information and smart ass responses? Enjoy:
Two red deer stags fight with their antlers. (Getty Images/iStockphoto)

articles.title_orig: US petrol prices dip ahead of midterms as voters eye costs
articles.title_zh: US petrol prices dip ahead of midterms as voters eye costs
articles.content_orig:
Petrol prices have dipped amid renewed diplomatic efforts to end the US-Israel war on Iran, but remain high ahead of the United States midterm elections , as the cost of living remains a central issue for voters.
On Monday, the average price for a gallon (3.78 litres) of regular petrol was $4.17, according to the American Automobile Association (AAA), which tracks daily petrol prices. That is down 12 cents from this time last week and 23 cents from a month ago.
By comparison, prices were $3.04 this time a year ago and $2.98 on February 28, when the US and Israel first struck Iran.
Diesel fuel prices remain high at $6.29 per gallon, but that is down 6 cents from this time last week. Diesel prices climbed above $6 a gallon for the first time in September before topping out at $6.53.
The average petrol price of President Donald Trump’s second term to date was set to exceed $3.46 a gallon on Monday, surpassing the previous record for a presidential administration set under former President Joe Biden, according to a Financial Times analysis of federal data.
Oil prices are continuing to fall, down 6 percent on Monday as diplomatic efforts to end the US-Israel war on Iran continued following in-person talks in Qatar over the weekend.
“Oil markets down significantly this morning after Trump signalled he favoured negotiations and not new attacks on Iran,” Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis at GasBuddy, said in a post on X. “Oil down [approximately] 5%, wholesale gasoline and diesel pointing to roughly 16 [cents per gallon] decline. The national average could fall under $4 a gallon in the next week barring a course change.”
Cost-of-living issues remain top of mind for US voters as they head to the polls. An Associated Press-NORC poll last month found that a majority of Americans believe addressing cost-of-living issues should be a priority for Congress, including 78 percent of Republicans and 89 percent of Democrats.
“Once this conflict comes to an end, gas prices will drop drastically, and the Iranian terrorist regime will not have a nuclear weapon,” White House spokesperson Taylor Rogers told Al Jazeera. “Protecting America’s national security from threats by a radical terrorist regime that has chanted ‘Death to America’ for 47 years was the right thing to do – and President Trump is the only president who has had the courage to do it.”
Rogers added, “Thanks to the exceptional work of the US military, more oil is now flowing out of the Persian Gulf than before the Iran conflict began.”
On Wall Street, oil and gas giant stocks were trending downward in midday trading. ConocoPhillips was down 3.7 percent, Chevron 2.3 percent and ExxonMobil 3.3 percent.
The major US indices more broadly were in positive territory. The Nasdaq was up 0.7 percent, the S&P 500 0.6 percent and the Dow Jones Industrial Average 1 percent.

Hello, this is Leonie Kidd with today's edition of Morning Squawk.
Markets are ready to turn over a new leaf in November, with futures higher after closing out a tough October.
This week brings a raft of market moments, with more Magnificent Seven earnings, the midterms, and a payrolls data day on Friday.
Buckle up, it's another big week.
Oil prices are at the center of the price action, with both Brent and WTI falling over 4% in early trade.
The move comes as negotiators renewed diplomatic efforts to ease tensions with Iran. According to Reuters , a draft proposal is being circulated after another round of talks in Doha on Sunday.
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters this weekend that President Donald Trump would prefer to resolve the war "diplomatically," adding that "...if we needed to do something militarily, we would have the ability to do it, and we really have everything we need to be successful. But we would prefer to do it peacefully."
Futures are moving higher, looking set to start November on a positive note after the worst month for the Nasdaq 100 in a year .
The chip stocks are supporting the gains, with a strong handover from Asia. Shares in SK Hynix and Samsung rose sharply during overnight trading.

Apple will be hoping to bring the shine back to the Magnificent Seven after last week's rough run for technology stocks. So far, the stock is the group's best performer — up 28% year-to-date — but expectations are sky-high.
CNBC's MacKenzie Sigalos will report from Cupertino as CEO John Ternus hosts his first earnings call at the helm.

CNBC's coverage will continue throughout the day with a focus on the economy.
'Pop-up' super PACs pour $637 million into 2026 midterm races

But voters still cannot see who supplied the money.

articles.title_orig: Marvell doubles down on AI boom with costly $115 billion Lumentum deal
articles.title_zh: Marvell doubles down on AI boom with costly $115 billion Lumentum deal
articles.content_orig:
Marvell Technology Chairman and CEO Matt Murphy and Lumentum CEO Michael Hurlston detail their record-breaking merger and how their ‘shared vision’ will create a category leader in AI connectivity on ‘The Claman Countdown.’
Marvell Technology chairman and CEO Matt Murphy said the chipmaker’s historic $115 billion acquisition of Lumentum is a "once in a generation’ opportunity to unite two of the most dominating companies in the AI boom and create a "category leader."
Appearing alongside Lumentum CEO Michael Hurlston on "The Claman Countdown," Murphy detailed the companies’ record-breaking merger on Monday, predicting that the transaction will cement Marvell’s position at the forefront of AI connectivity.
"It's very rare that you can find two companies of the caliber of Lumentum and Marvell that are number one in their respective areas that find a moment in time where you can combine and create a category leader in a new category," he told anchor Liz Claman.
AMERICA AND CHINA ARE FIGHTING FOR THE FUTURE OF AI — CHIPS ARE THE BATTLEFIELD
The race to build AI infrastructure is accelerating as concerns grow over centralized technological power. (Noah Berger / Getty Images)
"This AI connectivity is going to be as consequential as… the compute category, or the memory category, the fab category, and the IP licensing category."
Murphy's comments follow the announcement of Marvell’s agreement to acquire Lumentum in a landmark $115 billion transaction, marking the largest merger between two publicly traded companies. The deal will unite two massive AI enablers, equipped with electrical and optical expertise, to address connectivity requirements for next-generation AI infrastructure .
MASSIVE AI BOOM PUTS ONE OF AMERICA’S OLDEST MANUFACTURERS ON PATH TO DOUBLE IN SIZE, CEO SAYS
"Both companies.are executing phenomenally well. And what we see, Liz, is a multiplying effect, where we're gonna do much better together in two years than we would on a standalone basis," Hurlston predicted.
Under the terms of the all-stock agreement, Lumentum shareholders will receive 4.5 shares of Marvell common stock for each share held, according to Marvell’s announcement.
"It’s really a historic day for the two companies," Murphy said. "We're putting together basically the best-in-class leader in AI connectivity technology for semiconductors with the leader in photonics. And it is something that hasn't been done before."
Marvell Technology Chairman and CEO Matt Murphy (Right) appeared alongside Lumentum CEO Michael Hurlston (Left) on "The Claman Countdown" on Monday. (Left (Takaaki Iwabu/Bloomberg via Getty Images), Right (Lam Yik Fei/Bloomberg via Getty Images) / Getty Images)
Marvell designs artificial intelligence chips and technology that powers data centers , while Lumentum designs lasers and other optical components that use light to transmit data between chips and servers.
Murphy said Lumentum and Marvell, both headquartered in Northern California, have a "shared vision" and detailed how he believes the two tech companies will work better together than apart.
IT TOOK 3 MONTHS TO GET INSIDE THIS MASSIVE TEXAS DATA CENTER — HERE’S WHAT WE SAW
"Together, because of the additional opportunity we see with each other, there's an opportunity to really outperform as a combined company," the Marvell CEO said.
Murphy, who said the merger has received "tremendous support" from hyperscalers, told FOX Business that he expects "significant" revenue synergies and other benefits once the companies are joined together.
AI chip giant Nvidia is a strategic investor in both Lumentum, which has a market value of around $76 billion, and Marvell, with a value of roughly $172 billion.
The Marvell-Lumentum deal has garnered "super positive" feedback from Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, Hurlston said. (Getty )
CLICK HERE TO GET FOX BUSINESS ON THE GO
Hurlston told FOX Business that Murphy discussed the potential Lumentum acquisition with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang early in the process, adding that reaction from Nvidia has been "super positive."
"Nvidia is invested in Marvell, Nvidia is invested in Lumentum. We think we can actually bring a lot more product to bear to Nvidia a lot more quickly in this combination," Hurlston said.

articles.title_orig: China Lays Out Four Missions Leading to a Crewed Moon Landing
articles.title_zh: China Lays Out Four Missions Leading to a Crewed Moon Landing
articles.content_orig:
China has published a mission-by-mission schedule for landing astronauts on the Moon before 2030, about a year behind NASA's 2028 target, Ars Technica reported. It is the most detailed public account so far of the country's lunar program.
Wang Xiang presented the plan on October 31 at the 7th Manned Space Academic Conference. He is deputy chief designer of China's Manned Space Program and chief designer of its lunar exploration project.
The two-day event at Beihang University was hosted by the China Manned Space Agency. It drew more than 800 experts and scholars, BigGo Finance reported.
Slides from the presentation list these steps, according to Ars Technica:
BigGo Finance summarised the 2028 to 2030 window differently. It said Wenchang, the launch site in Hainan, will host three uncrewed lunar orbit verification missions and one crewed landing.
Three astronauts would make the trip, with two going down to the surface, Shattered reported, citing Chinese state media. The third would stay in orbit aboard Mengzhou.
China lacks a rocket as powerful as the Saturn V. So the crew ship and lander launch separately. Shattered said this lets controllers confirm the lander reached lunar orbit before the crew commits to the trip.
After docking in lunar orbit, the two astronauts move into the lander and descend. They lift off, dock with Mengzhou a second time and return to Earth in the spacecraft, BigGo Finance said.
Development is under way on the lander, a moonwalk spacesuit and a crewed lunar rover.
There is no Apollo 8 or Artemis II equivalent in this plan. In those missions, a crew flies to the Moon and returns without landing, Ars Technica noted. Mengzhou will still carry astronauts to the Tiangong space station in low-Earth orbit.
In August 2025, the China Manned Space Agency tested a high-fidelity mock-up of the 26-ton Lanyue lander near Beijing. Tethers simulated lunar gravity. On February 11, Mengzhou passed a maximum dynamic pressure abort test and splashed down safely at sea.
BigGo Finance described it as China's first at-sea recovery of a crewed spacecraft.
Mengzhou has also arrived at Wenchang for the 2027 test flight. On October 22, the agency asked Chinese institutions to propose payloads for the uncrewed Lanyue flight. Shattered reported a March 1, 2027 deadline for those proposals.
It also said no firm date has been given for the crewed mission.
Ars Technica said NASA's schedule depends on lunar landers from SpaceX and Blue Origin. A US landing could slip to 2030 or later. NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman has cancelled the Lunar Gateway space station.
He has also cancelled planned upgrades to the Space Launch System rocket.
Shattered reported that Artemis III is now a crewed Earth-orbit test in 2027. The first landing moves to Artemis IV, targeted for early 2028.

articles.title_zh: As peacekeepers leave Western Sahara, refugees yearn to end a half-century wait
articles.content_orig:
The conflict pits Morocco, which considers the region its own, against the Algeria-backed Polisario Front, which seeks a separate state
At 51, Binina Mohamed is as old as the conflict that drove her from the Western Sahara region into a refugee camp in southern Algeria, where she has spent her life among tens of thousands of others facing a similar fate.
The confrontation over her native land, often described as Africa’s longest-running territorial dispute, was brought back into focus this weekend by a UN Security ‌Council row that led to the end of a decades-old peacekeeping mission there.
The Western Sahara conflict pits Morocco, which considers the territory its own, against the Algeria-backed Polisario Front, a political and military organisation that has been seeking a separate state there since the departure of former colonial power Spain in 1976. Peacekeepers have watched over the territory since 1991, when the UN brokered a ceasefire ending years of guerrilla warfare between the two sides.

articles.title_orig: China Tech Stocks Get Fresh Lifeline From Beijing
articles.title_zh: China Tech Stocks Get Fresh Lifeline From Beijing
articles.content_orig:
Alibaba BABA , JD.com JD and PDD Holdings PDD moved higher in U.S. premarket trading Monday after Chinese regulators signaled a fresh effort to stabilize the country's battered stock market.
The move follows an 8.5% October drop in the CSI 300 , its worst monthly performance since early 2016. The benchmark had also fallen for 12 consecutive weeks, according to TipRanks.
Beijing is now stepping in with more liquidity.
The People's Bank of China said it will conduct a new swap operation Tuesday that could inject more than 100 billion yuan, or roughly $15 billion , into the equity market. Thirty-one brokerages and fund companies have already applied for quotas worth more than 100 billion yuan.
The swap facility allows securities firms, insurers and fund managers to exchange eligible assets for more liquid central-bank assets, giving them additional capacity to buy stocks.
China is also making its relending program for share repurchases and stake increases a long-term mechanism , while cutting the program's interest rate to 1% from 1.25% .
Regulators are applying pressure directly as well.
The China Securities Regulatory Commission urged major index constituents and leading technology companies to actively buy back shares , while also encouraging newer ETFs and fund managers to increase equity exposure during the downturn. Officials are separately studying whether to ease margin rules to improve market liquidity.
The policy response helped lift sentiment Monday, with the Shanghai Composite gaining 1.1% and the CSI 300 also moving higher.
Alibaba, JD and PDD have been caught in the broader decline as investors grapple with weak Chinese consumption, persistent property-sector problems and pressure across technology shares.
I think the key point here is that Beijing is sending a clearer message that it does not want the equity selloff to spiral.
For Alibaba, JD and PDD, that matters because their stocks have increasingly been trading on macro sentiment and policy risk, not just company fundamentals.
The latest measures can improve liquidity and potentially put a floor under sentiment.
But they do not fix the underlying issues by themselves.
China still needs stronger consumption, better economic momentum and more confidence in corporate earnings for the rally to become durable.
For investors, the key things to watch are how much of the new liquidity is actually deployed, whether corporate buybacks accelerate, and whether China follows these market-support steps with broader fiscal or economic stimulus .
The immediate signal is supportive.
The harder question is whether Beijing can turn that support into a lasting recovery.

articles.title_orig: How China Might Target US Midterms - Center for European Policy Analysis (CEPA)
articles.title_zh: How China Might Target US Midterms - Center for European Policy Analysis (CEPA)
articles.content_orig:
No research shows Chinese propaganda or disinformation playing a pivotal role in the midterm elections, particularly when compared to Russia’s aggressive attempts. Yet significant blind spots exist. If it desired, Beijing is well-positioned to shape political debate through the WeChat app and through Chinese AI models.
Rather than shifting control of Congress, Beijing’s goal would likely be to reduce the presence of known Communist Party critics, particularly those serving in the Congressional-Executive Commission on China. Created by Congress in October 2000, the Commission monitors Chinese human rights and rule of law.
Several competitive races feature Commission members, including former Senator Sherrod Brown in Ohio and current Commission Chair Dan Sullivan in Alaska. House races in Iowa and Virginia involve current Commission members Zach Nunn and Jen Kiggans. Ashley Hinson, who is running for the Senate in Iowa, is on the House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party, another Congressional body critical of the regime.
Texas looks particularly sensitive for a different reason. WeChat , a messaging and multi-function app, has an estimated 1.5 million US users, concentrated in states with large Chinese American populations. Chinese Americans make up roughly one percent of Texas’s population .
Chinese state-sponsored censorship on WeChat is well-documented. A 2025 University of Texas study based on interviews with 20 Chinese Americans in Texas detailed how political misinformation circulates on the platform. One young interviewee described how her father read that an Asian American woman had been elected mayor of Boston months before the actual election.
“He just accepts everything he reads, and then he just forwards it,” she said. “My mother-in-law, too.”
Cultural and social pressures reduce willingness to correct misinformation in family or friend groups. “It doesn’t feel right for me to talk bad to my elders, especially in the group chat setting,” a 19-year-old Chinese American explained.
In this environment, the app is powerful. “A lot of people don’t know who to vote for, so they are easily swayed,” another interviewee commented. “It is a big political platform, and a lot of people will just blindly follow.”
The 2026 elections are the first to take place in an environment where AI chatbots are widely available. About one-fifth of Americans plan to use AI tools to help learn about candidates or inform voting decisions, according to a recent survey . Most will turn to American models such as ChatGPT, Claude, Grok, or Perplexity, but many US developers are increasingly relying on Chinese-origin models such as DeepSeek and Qwen, allowing them to enter the US information environment.
These models reflect the Chinese government’s official stances on domestic politics and human rights. Censorship and propaganda have also been found in responses to questions about US press freedom and elections.
One study examined Chinese AI models’ responses to questions about the upcoming US elections. Conducted by a research group based in Europe, researchers tested seven AI models (five US and two Chinese) with a set of 20 polling-style questions.
All models proved relatively consistent and offered mixed results in terms of partisan preferences. The two Chinese models did not diverge sharply from their US counterparts in their responses. DeepSeek, for example, selected the Democratic option on two questions about which party’s candidate it would select for Congress and which party it prefers to control Congress. So did Claude and Perplexity (99% on one of the questions). By contrast, Qwen chose Democrats 55% and 75% of the time, respectively.
The results are striking for what they show about the leeway allowed the Chinese models to comment on US versus Chinese politics. DeepSeek offered critical assessments of the US president’s job performance. Asking the same questions about Chinese President Xi Jinping would almost certainly produce refusals or strictly glowing reviews.
Major holes remain in our understanding of where and how Chinese Communist Party-linked electoral influence could be occurring. Researchers, election monitors, and others focused on election integrity should address these gaps — particularly before the 2028 elections.
Sarah Cook is founder of China Rights Analytics and Advising LLC and author of the UnderReported China newsletter.

articles.title_orig: 'Exceptionally horrific strike' — Russian bombs hit school used as humanitarian aid center in Zaporizhzhia Oblast, killing 26
articles.title_zh: 'Exceptionally horrific strike' — Russian bombs hit school used as humanitarian aid center in Zaporizhzhia Oblast, killing 26
articles.content_orig:
Video shows smoke rising from Komyshuvakha blast crater
At least 26 people were killed after Russian bombs hit an aid distribution centre, in an attack that Ukraine's leader has called "utterly horrific".
Five people were injured and 27 initially reported missing after at least nine 3,000kg aerial bombs hit the village of Komyshuvakha in the southern Zaporizhzhia region, regional head Mykhailo Semikin said.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said that after the first strike on the local school "used for humanitarian needs", there was a second attack on the place where people were sheltering.
He posted a video showing a huge crater left after Monday's attack, and rescuer teams searching through the rubble.
The Russian military has not publicly commented.
There are fears that the death toll will rise further as a number of people are still under the rubble
Zelensky initially put the death toll at 18, but Ukraine's state emergencies service DSNS later said 24 people, including two rescuers and four police officers, were confirmed to have been killed.
In his video address late on Monday, Zelensky said 26 people were now known to have died.
He earlier said that "the Russians could not have been unaware that the local residents who remained in Komyshuvakha received humanitarian aid there every week" on Monday.
"This is yet another proof that Russia does not want any de-escalation."
He said that after a recent successful joint Russian-Ukrainian operation to evacuate civilians from the Russia-occupied southern city of Oleshky during a temporary ceasefire brokered by US First Lady Melania Trump, "there was a moment when the next steps could show that peace is possible".
"With such killings, Russia is sending the exact opposite signal - Russia is counting on further killings," Zelensky said.
The Russian strikes left a huge crater where Ukrainian officials say people were sheltering
Meanwhile, Semikin described the Russian attack as a "terrible tragedy" for the village, confirming that "people are still under the rubble".
He said rescue teams were working at the scene, but they had been forced to halt their operation a number of times because of Russian drone attacks in the area.
A day of mourning has been declared for Tuesday across the entire Zaporizhzhia region.
Russian President Vladimir Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
Teams from Ukraine, Russia and the US are due to resume peace talks in the next few days after negotiations were suspended in February, with Moscow stepping up attacks as Kyiv virtually ran out of Western-supplied interceptors to defend against missiles.
However, no major breakthrough is expected at the talks that are likely to be held in Abu Dhabi, the United Arab Emirates.

articles.title_orig: Oil prices slide as hopes rise for potential US-Iran diplomatic breakthrough
articles.title_zh: Oil prices slide as hopes rise for potential US-Iran diplomatic breakthrough
articles.content_orig:
Crude oil prices fell sharply Monday as the presidents of the U.S. and Iran signalled they are open to a diplomatic solution to the conflict that has disrupted energy markets for eight months.
U.S. West Texas Intermediate futures shed 7.4% to close at $96.46 a barrel, the biggest daily loss since July 27. Brent crude , the international benchmark, lost 7.6% to settle at $104.77 a barrel.
President Donald Trump told reporters Monday that Iran wants to "make a deal and that could happen." U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said over the weekend that Trump prefers not to use military force against Iran and would like to resolve the conflict diplomatically.
Trump has previously said that he will not attack Iran before the U.S. midterms. But the oil market had priced in the risk of a major military escalation after the elections, gaining more than 10% in October.
The oil market has sold off during previous phases of the war on rumors of a possible settlement, only for the conflict to subsequently escalate and spike prices again.
Trump "hasn't made a decision" on whether to strike Iran again, Rubio told reporters.
"What the president expresses to you is incredible confidence that if we needed to do something militarily, we would have the ability to do it," the secretary of State said. "But we would prefer to do it peacefully."
Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian said Tehran is seeking to resolve problems through dialogue, according to state-owned Islamic Republic News Agency . Iran's Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei has granted the government certain authorities to do this, Pezeshkian said.
Iran's foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, said an agreement with the U.S. is possible if Washington "demonstrates goodwill" and is "truly seeking a peaceful solution," according to IRNA.
Araghchi said mediators are discussing the proposal Iran made during the United Nations General Assembly in September. Tehran expects the U.S. to lift sanctions, reduce its military presence in the region to previous levels and lift the blockade, the foreign minister said.
But Khamenei on Saturday called for Tehran's armed forces to meet "any level or type of threat" with "an immediate, impactful, and geographically unrestricted response."
Reports about diplomatic efforts will have a big impact on crude oil prices because much of the market's recent gains were risk premium in anticipation of a possible escalation, according to Ryan McKay, director of commodity strategy at TD Securities.
"With that said, so long as there is no concrete conclusion to the war, and tanker and Houthi attacks remain prevalent, we do not anticipate a complete erosion of the risk premium via diplomacy headlines alone," McKay said.
— CNBC's Lim Hui Jie contributed to this report.
